(2.9)

The product estimates (
2.7
), (
2.8
), and (
2.9
)
follow easily from the definition (
2.2
) of the paraproduct
and the resonant product.
See
[
2
,
47
]
for details of the proofs in the non-periodic case
(which can be easily extended to the current periodic setting).

We also recall the following product estimate from
[
35
,
6
]
.

Lemma 2.3
.

Let
s>0
.

(i)

Let
1<p_{j},q_{j},r\leq\infty
,
j=1,2
such that
\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{p_{j}}+\frac{1}{q_{j}}
.
Then, we have

\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s}(fg)\|_{L^{r}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}\lesssim\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s}f\|_{L^{p_{1}}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}\|g\|_{L^{q_{1}}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}+\|f\|_{L^{p_{2}}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s}g\|_{L^{q_{2}}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}.

(ii)

Let
1<p\leq\infty
and
1<q,r<\infty
such that
s\geq 3\big(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{r}\big)

and
q,r^{\prime}\geq p^{\prime}
.
Then, we have

\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{-s}(fg)\|_{L^{r}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}\lesssim\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{-s}f\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s}g\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}.

2.2.
On discrete convolutions

Next, we recall the following basic lemma on a discrete convolution.

Lemma 2.4
.

Let
d\geq 1
and
\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}
satisfy

\alpha+\beta>d\qquad\text{and}\qquad\alpha<d.

Then, we have

\sum_{n=n_{1}+n_{2}}\frac{1}{\langle n_{1}\rangle^{\alpha}\langle n_{2}\rangle^{\beta}}\lesssim\langle n\rangle^{-\alpha+\lambda}

for any
n\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}
,
where
\lambda=\max(d-\beta,0)
when
\beta\neq d
and
\lambda=\varepsilon
when
\beta=d
for any
\varepsilon>0
.

Lemma
2.4
follows
from elementary computations.
See, for example,

[
30
, Lemma 4.2]
and
[
49
, Lemma 4.1]
.

2.3.
Tools from stochastic analysis

We conclude this section by recalling useful lemmas
from stochastic analysis.
See
[
69
,
51
]
for basic definitions.
Let
(H,B,\mu)
be an abstract Wiener space.
Namely,
\mu
is a Gaussian measure on a separable Banach space
B

with
H\subset B
as its Cameron-Martin space.
Given a complete orthonormal system
\{e_{j}\}_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\subset B^{*}
of
H^{*}=H
,
we define a polynomial chaos of order

k
to be an element of the form
\prod_{j=1}^{\infty}H_{k_{j}}(\langle x,e_{j}\rangle)
,
where
x\in B
,
k_{j}\neq 0
for only finitely many
j
’s,
k=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}k_{j}
,

H_{k_{j}}
is the Hermite polynomial of degree
k_{j}
,
and
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle=\vphantom{|}_{B}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{B^{*}}
denotes the
B
-
B^{*}
duality pairing.
We then
denote the closure of
polynomial chaoses of order
k

under
L^{2}(B,\mu)
by
\mathcal{H}_{k}
.
The elements in
\mathcal{H}_{k}

are called homogeneous Wiener chaoses of order
k
.
We also set

\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\leq k}=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{k}\mathcal{H}_{j}

for
k\in\mathbb{N}
.

As a consequence
of the hypercontractivity of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck
semigroup due to Nelson
[
50
]
,
we have the following Wiener chaos estimate

[
70
, Theorem I.22]
.
See also
[
71
, Proposition 2.4]
.

Lemma 2.5
.

Let
k\in\mathbb{N}
.
Then, we have

\|X\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\leq(p-1)^{\frac{k}{2}}\|X\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}

for any finite
p\geq 2

and any
X\in\mathcal{H}_{\leq k}
.

Lastly, we recall the following orthogonality
relation for the Hermite polynomials.
See
[
51
, Lemma 1.1.1]
.

Lemma 2.6
.

Let
f
and
g
be jointly Gaussian random variables with mean zero
and variances
\sigma_{f}

and
\sigma_{g}
.
Then, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[H_{k}(f;\sigma_{f})H_{\ell}(g;\sigma_{g})\big]=\delta_{k\ell}k!\big\{\mathbb{E}[fg]\big\}^{k},

where

H_{k}(x,\sigma)
denotes the Hermite polynomial of degree
k
with variance parameter
\sigma
.

3.
Construction of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
in the weakly nonlinear regime

In this section, we present the construction
of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure in the weakly nonlinear regime (Theorem
1.8
(i)).
Our proof is based on the variational approach
introduced by Barashkov and Gubinelli
[
3
]
.
See the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
)
below.
In Subsection
3.1
,
we briefly go over the setup of the variational
formulation for a partition function.
In Subsection
3.2
,
we first establish the uniform exponential integrability (
1.27
)
and then prove tightness of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\rho_{N}
in (
1.25
),
which implies weak convergence of a subsequence.
In Subsection
3.3
,
we follow the approach introduced in our previous work
[
54
]

and prove uniqueness of the limiting
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure,
thus establishing weak convergence of the entire sequence
\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
.
Finally,
in Subsection
3.4
,
we show that the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
and the base Gaussian free field
\mu
in (
1.16
) are mutually singular.
While our proof of singularity of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure is inspired by the discussion in Section 4 of
[
4
]
,
we directly prove singularity without referring to a shifted measure.
In Appendix
A
, we show that the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure is indeed absolutely continuous with respect
to the shifted measure

\Law(Y(1)+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}(1)+\mathcal{W}(1))
,
where
\Law(Y(1))=\mu
,

\mathfrak{Z}=\mathfrak{Z}(Y)
is the limit of the quadratic process
\mathfrak{Z}^{N}
defined in (
3.11
),
and the auxiliary quintic process
\mathcal{W}=\mathcal{W}(Y)
is defined in (
A.1
).

3.1.
Boué-Dupuis variational formula

Let
W(t)
be the cylindrical
Wiener process on
L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
(with respect to the underlying probability measure
\mathbb{P}
):

\displaystyle W(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}B_{n}(t)e_{n},

(3.1)

where

\{B_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}

is defined by

B_{n}(t)=\langle\xi,\mathbf{1}_{[0,t]}\cdot e_{n}\rangle_{x,t}
.
Here,
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{x,t}
denotes
the duality pairing on
\mathbb{T}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}
.
Note that we have, for any
n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}
,

\text{Var}(B_{n}(t))=\mathbb{E}\Big[\langle\xi,\mathbf{1}_{[0,t]}\cdot e_{n}\rangle_{x,t}\overline{\langle\xi,\mathbf{1}_{[0,t]}\cdot e_{n}\rangle_{x,t}}\Big]=\|\mathbf{1}_{[0,t]}\cdot e_{n}\|_{L^{2}_{x,t}}^{2}=t.

As a result,
we see that
\{B_{n}\}_{n\in\Lambda_{0}}
is a family of mutually independent complex-valued
Brownian motions conditioned so that
B_{-n}=\overline{B_{n}}
,
n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}
.
15
15

15

In particular,
B_{0}
is a standard real-valued Brownian motion.

We then define a centered Gaussian process
Y(t)

by

\displaystyle Y(t)=\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}W(t).

(3.2)

Then,
we have
\Law(Y(1))=\mu
.
By setting
Y_{N}=\pi_{N}Y
,
we have
\Law(Y_{N}(1))=(\pi_{N})_{\#}\mu
.
In particular,
we have
\mathbb{E}[Y_{N}(1)^{2}]=\sigma_{N}
,
where
\sigma_{N}
is as in (
1.22
).

Next, let
\mathbb{H}_{a}
denote the space of drifts, which are the progressively measurable processes
belonging to

L^{2}([0,1];L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
,
\mathbb{P}
-almost surely.
For later use, we also define

\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}

to be the space of drifts, which are the progressively measurable processes
belonging to

L^{2}([0,1];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
,
\mathbb{P}
-almost surely.
Namely, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}=\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}\mathbb{H}_{a}.

(3.3)

We now state the Boué-Dupuis variational formula
[
8
,
77
]
;
in particular, see Theorem 7 in
[
77
]
.
See also Theorem 2 in
[
3
]
.

Lemma 3.1
.

Let
Y(t)=\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}W(t)
be as in (
3.2
).
Fix
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
Suppose that
F:C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\to\mathbb{R}

is measurable such that
\mathbb{E}\big[|F(Y_{N}(1))|^{p}\big]<\infty

and
\mathbb{E}\big[|e^{-F(Y_{N}(1))}|^{q}\big]<\infty
for some
1<p,q<\infty
with
\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1
.
Then, we have

\displaystyle-\log\mathbb{E}\Big[e^{-F(Y_{N}(1))}\Big]=\inf_{\theta\in\mathbb{H}_{a}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[F(Y_{N}(1)+\pi_{N}I(\theta)(1))+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg],

(3.4)

where
I(\theta)
is defined by

\displaystyle I(\theta)(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}\theta(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}.

(3.5)

Lemma
3.1
plays a fundamental role
in almost every step of the argument presented in this section
and Section
4
.

We state a useful lemma on the pathwise regularity estimates of

:\!Y^{k}(t)\!:
and
I(\theta)(1)
.

Lemma 3.2
.

(i)

For
k=1,2
, any finite
p\geq 2
, and
\varepsilon>0
,

:\!Y_{N}^{k}(t)\!:
converges to
:\!Y^{k}(t)\!:
in
L^{p}(\Omega;\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{k}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))

and also almost surely in
\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{k}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
.
Moreover, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\Big[\|:\!Y_{N}^{k}(t)\!:\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{k}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{p}\Big]&\lesssim p^{\frac{k}{2}}<\infty,\\
\end{split}

(3.6)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
and
t\in[0,1]
.
We also have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\|:\!Y_{N}^{2}(t)\!:\|_{H^{-1}}^{2}\Big]\sim t^{2}\log N

(3.7)

for any
t\in[0,1]
.

(ii)

For any
N\in\mathbb{N}
, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Y_{N}^{3}(1)\!:dx\bigg]=0.\end{split}

(iii)
For any
\theta\in\mathbb{H}_{a}
, we have

\displaystyle\|I(\theta)(1)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\leq\int_{0}^{1}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}dt.

Proof.

The bound (
3.6
) for
\varepsilon>0
follows
from the Wiener chaos estimate (Lemma
2.5
), Lemma
2.6
,
and then carrying out summations, using Lemma
2.4
.
See, for example,
[
35
,
36
]
.
As for (
3.7
),
proceeding as in the proof of Lemma 2.5 in
[
63
]

with Lemma
2.6
, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}&\Big[\|:\!Y_{N}^{2}(t)\!:\|_{H^{-1}}^{2}\Big]\\
&=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{1}{\langle n\rangle^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}_{x}\times\mathbb{T}^{3}_{y}}\mathbb{E}\Big[H_{2}(Y_{N}(x,t);t\sigma_{N})H_{2}(Y_{N}(y,t);t\sigma_{N})\Big]e_{n}(y-x)dxdy\\
&=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{t^{2}}{\langle n\rangle^{2}}\sum_{n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{\chi_{N}^{2}(n_{1})\chi_{N}^{2}(n_{2})}{\langle n_{1}\rangle^{2}\langle n_{2}\rangle^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}_{x}\times\mathbb{T}^{3}_{y}}e_{n_{1}+n_{2}-n}(x-y)dxdy\\
&=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{t^{2}}{\langle n\rangle^{2}}\sum_{n=n_{1}+n_{2}}\frac{\chi_{N}^{2}(n_{1})\chi_{N}^{2}(n_{2})}{\langle n_{1}\rangle^{2}\langle n_{2}\rangle^{2}},\end{split}

(3.8)

where
\chi_{N}(n_{j})
is as in (
1.20
).
The upper bound in (
3.7
) follows from applying Lemma
2.4

to (
3.8
).
As for the lower bound, we consider the contribution from
|n|\leq\frac{2}{3}N

and
\frac{1}{4}|n|\leq|n_{1}|\leq\frac{1}{2}|n|

(which implies
|n_{2}|\sim|n|
and
|n_{j}|\leq N
,
j=1,2
).
Then, from (
3.8
), we obtain

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\|:\!Y_{N}^{2}(t)\!:\|_{H^{-1}}^{2}\Big]\gtrsim\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\\
|n|\leq\frac{2}{3}N\end{subarray}}\frac{t^{2}}{\langle n\rangle^{3}}\sim t^{2}\log N,

which proves the lower bound in (
3.7
).
As for (ii), it follows from
recalling the definition
:\!Y_{N}^{3}(1)\!:\,=H_{3}(Y_{N}(1);\sigma_{N})

(with
\sigma_{N}
as in (
1.22
))
and
the orthogonality relation of the Hermite polynomials
(Lemma
2.6
with
k=3
and
\ell=0
).
Lastly,
the claim in (iii) follows from Minkowski’s integral inequality
and Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; see Lemma 4.7 in
[
38
]
.
∎

Remark 3.3
.

In
[
38
,
58
]
,
a slightly different (and weaker) variational formula
was used. See also Lemma 1 in
[
3
]
.
Given a drift
\theta\in\mathbb{H}_{a}
,
we define the measure
\mathbb{Q}_{\theta}

whose Radon-Nikodym derivative with
respect to
\mathbb{P}
is given by the following stochastic exponential:

\displaystyle\frac{d\mathbb{Q}_{\theta}}{d\mathbb{P}}=e^{\int_{0}^{1}\langle\theta(t),dW(t)\rangle-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}^{2}dt},

where
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle
stands for the usual inner product on
L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
.
Let
\mathbb{H}_{c}
denote the subspace of
\mathbb{H}_{a}
consisting of drifts such that
\mathbb{Q}_{\theta}(\Omega)=1
.
Then, the (weaker) variational formula
used in
[
38
,
58
]

is given by (
3.4
),
where the infimum is taken over
\mathbb{H}_{c}\subset\mathbb{H}_{a}

and we replace

Y
and
\mathbb{E}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}

by
Y_{\theta}=Y-I(\theta)
and
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}_{\theta}}
.
Here,

\mathbb{E}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}
and
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}_{\theta}}

denote
expectations with respect to the underlying probability measure
\mathbb{P}

and the measure
\mathbb{Q}_{\theta}
, respectively.
In such a formulation,

Y_{\theta}
and the measure
\mathbb{Q}_{\theta}
depend on a drift
\theta
.
This, however, is not suitable for our purpose,
since we construct a drift
\theta
in (
3.4
) depending on
Y
.

3.2.
Uniform exponential integrability and tightness

In this subsection,
we first prove the uniform exponential integrability (
1.27
)
via the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
).
Then,
we establish tightness of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
.

As in the case of
the
\Phi^{4}_{3}
-measure
studied in
[
3
]

(see also Section 6 in
[
54
]
),
we need to introduce a
further renormalization than the standard Wick renormalization (see (
1.24
)).
As a result,
the resulting
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
is singular with respect to the base Gaussian free field
\mu
;
see Subsection
3.4
.
We point out that this extra renormalization
appears only at the level of the measure
and thus does not affect the dynamical problem, at least locally in time.
16
16

16

As mentioned in Section
1
,
this singularity of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
causes an additional difficulty for the globalization problem.

In the following, we use the following short-hand notations:
Y_{N}(t)=\pi_{N}Y(t)
,

\Theta(t)=I(\theta)(t)
, and
\Theta_{N}(t)=\pi_{N}\Theta(t)

with
Y_{N}=Y_{N}(1)
and
\Theta_{N}=\Theta_{N}(1)
.
We also use

Y=Y(1)
and
\Theta=\Theta(1)
.

Let us first explain
the second renormalization introduced in (
1.24
).
Let
R_{N}
be as in (
1.23
)
and set

\displaystyle\widetilde{Z}_{N}=\int e^{-R_{N}(u)}d\mu(u).

By Lemma
3.1
,
we can express the partition function
\widetilde{Z}_{N}

as

\displaystyle-\log\widetilde{Z}_{N}=\inf_{\theta\in\mathbb{H}_{a}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[R_{N}(Y+\Theta)+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg].

By expanding the cubic Wick power, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!(Y_{N}+\Theta_{N})^{3}\!:dx&=-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Y_{N}^{3}\!:dx-\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:\Theta_{N}dx\\
&\quad-\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Theta_{N}^{2}dx-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Theta_{N}^{3}dx.\end{split}

(3.9)

In view of
Lemma
3.2
,
the first term on the right-hand side vanishes
under an expectation,
while
we can estimate the third and fourth terms on
the right-hand side of (
3.9
)
(see Lemma
3.5
).
As we see below,
the second term turns out to be divergent
(and does not vanish under an expectation).
From the Ito product formula, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\!:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:\,\Theta_{N}dx\bigg]=\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Y_{N}^{2}(t)\!:\,\dot{\Theta}_{N}(t)dxdt\bigg],

(3.10)

where we have

\dot{\Theta}_{N}(t)=\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}\pi_{N}\theta(t)

in view of (
3.5
).
Define
\mathfrak{Z}^{N}
with
\mathfrak{Z}^{N}(0)=0
by its time derivative:

\displaystyle\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}^{N}(t)=(1-\Delta)^{-1}\!:\!Y_{N}^{2}(t)\!:

(3.11)

and set

\mathfrak{Z}_{N}=\pi_{N}\mathfrak{Z}^{N}
.
Then, we
perform a
change of variables:

\displaystyle\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)=\dot{\Theta}(t)-\sigma\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}(t)

(3.12)

and set
\Upsilon_{N}=\pi_{N}\Upsilon^{N}
.
From (
3.10
), (
3.11
), and (
3.12
),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:\Theta_{N}dx+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]-\alpha_{N},\end{split}

(3.13)

where the divergent constant
\alpha_{N}
is given by

\displaystyle\alpha_{N}=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]\longrightarrow\infty,

(3.14)

as
N\to\infty
.
The divergence in (
3.14
)
can be easily seen from the spatial regularity

1-\varepsilon
of
\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}(t)=(1-\Delta)^{-1}\!:\!Y_{N}^{2}(t)\!:

(with a uniform bound in
N\in\mathbb{N}
). See Lemma
3.2
.

In view of the discussion above,
we define
R_{N}^{\diamond}
as in (
1.24
),
which removes the divergent constant
\alpha_{N}
in (
3.13
).
Then,
from (
1.26
) and the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
),
we have

-\log Z_{N}=\inf_{\theta\in\mathbb{H}_{a}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[R_{N}^{\diamond}(Y+\Theta)+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]

(3.15)

for any
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
By setting

\mathcal{W}_{N}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\bigg[R_{N}^{\diamond}(Y+\Theta)+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\theta(t)\|_{L^{2}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg],

(3.16)

it follows from
(
1.23
) with
\gamma=3
,
(
1.24
), (
3.9
),
(
3.13
), and Lemma
3.2
(ii)
that

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{W}_{N}(\theta)&=\mathbb{E}\bigg[-\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Theta_{N}^{2}dx-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Theta_{N}^{3}dx\\
&\hphantom{XXii}+A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg].\end{split}

(3.17)

We also set

\displaystyle\Upsilon_{N}=\Upsilon_{N}(1)=\pi_{N}\Upsilon^{N}(1)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathfrak{Z}_{N}=\mathfrak{Z}_{N}(1)=\pi_{N}\mathfrak{Z}^{N}(1).

(3.18)

In view of the change of variables (
3.12
),
we have

\displaystyle\Theta_{N}=\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\pi_{N}\mathfrak{Z}_{N}=:\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N},\qquad\text{i.e.~}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}:=\pi_{N}\mathfrak{Z}_{N}.

(3.19)

Namely, the original drift
\theta
in (
3.15
)
depends on
Y
.
By the definition (
3.11
) and (
3.18
),

\mathfrak{Z}_{N}
is determined by
Y_{N}
.
Hence, in the following, we view

\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}
as a drift
and
study the minimization problem (
3.15
)
by first studying
each term in (
3.17
)
(where we now view
\mathcal{W}_{N}
as a function of
\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}
)
and
then taking an infimum in
\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}
,
where
\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}
is as in (
3.3
).
Our main goal is to show that

\mathcal{W}_{N}(\dot{\Upsilon}^{N})
in (
3.17
) is bounded away from
-\infty
,
uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
and
\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}
.

Remark 3.4
.

In this paper,
we work with
the cube frequency projector
\pi_{N}=\pi_{N}^{\text{cube}}
defined in (
1.19
),
satisfying
\pi_{N}^{2}=\pi_{N}
.
In view of (
3.18
) and (
3.19
), we have

\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}=\mathfrak{Z}_{N}
.
Nonetheless, we introduce the notation

\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}
in (
3.19
)
to indicate the modifications necessary
to consider the case of the smooth frequency projector
\pi_{N}^{\text{smooth}}

defined in (
1.42
), which does not satisfy

(\pi_{N}^{\text{smooth}})^{2}=\pi_{N}^{\text{smooth}}
.
This comment applies to the remaining part of the paper.

We first state two lemmas whose proofs are
presented at the end of this subsection.
While the first lemma is elementary,
the second lemma (Lemma
3.6
) requires
much more careful analysis,
reflecting the critical nature of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure.

Lemma 3.5
.

Let
A>0
and
0<|\sigma|<1
.
Then, there exist small
\varepsilon>0
and a constant
c>0

such that, for any
\delta>0
, there exists
C_{\delta}>0
such that

\displaystyle\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Theta_{N}^{2}dx\bigg|

\displaystyle\lesssim 1+C_{\delta}\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{c}+\delta\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+\delta\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{c},

(3.20)

\displaystyle\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Theta_{N}^{3}dx\bigg|

\displaystyle\lesssim 1+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{3},

(3.21)

and

\displaystyle\begin{split}A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:&+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}\geq\frac{A}{2}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(2Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}-\delta\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}\\
&\quad-C_{\delta,\sigma}\Bigg\{\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:dx\bigg|^{3}+\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{6}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{6}\Bigg\},\end{split}

(3.22)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
where

\Theta_{N}=\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}
as in (
3.19
).

The next lemma allows us to control the term

\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}
appearing in Lemma
3.5
.

Lemma 3.6
.

There exists
a non-negative random variable

B(\omega)

with
\mathbb{E}[B^{p}]\leq C_{p}<\infty
for any finite
p\geq 1

such that

\displaystyle\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}\lesssim\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(2Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+B(\omega),

(3.23)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
.

By assuming Lemmas
3.5

and
3.6
, we now prove
the uniform exponential integrability (
1.27
)
and tightness of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\rho_{N}
.

\bullet

Uniform exponential integrability:

In view of (
3.17
) and Lemma
3.6
,
define the positive part
\mathcal{U}_{N}
of
\mathcal{W}_{N}
by

\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{N}(\dot{\Upsilon}^{N})=\mathbb{E}\bigg[\frac{A}{2}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(2Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg].

(3.24)

As a corollary to Lemma
3.2
(i) with (
3.11
), we have,
for any finite
p\geq 1
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{p}\Big]\leq\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\!:\!Y_{N}^{2}(t)\!:\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-1-\varepsilon}}^{p}\Big]dt\lesssim p<\infty,

(3.25)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
Then, by applying
Lemmas
3.5
and

3.6
to (
3.17
)
together with
Lemma
3.2
and (
3.25
),
we obtain

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{W}_{N}(\dot{\Upsilon}^{N})&\geq-C_{0}+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\frac{A}{2}-c|\sigma|\Big)\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(2Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}\\
&\hphantom{XXXXXXX}+\Big(\frac{1}{2}-c|\sigma|\Big)\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]\\
&\geq-C_{0}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{10}\mathcal{U}_{N}(\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}),\end{split}

(3.26)

for any
0<|\sigma|<\sigma_{0}
,
provided
A=A(\sigma_{0})>0
is sufficiently large.
Noting that the estimate (
3.26
)
is uniform in
N\in\mathbb{N}

and
\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}
, we conclude that

\displaystyle\inf_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathcal{W}_{N}(\dot{\Upsilon}^{N})\geq\inf_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\bigg\{-C_{0}^{\prime}+\frac{1}{10}\mathcal{U}_{N}(\dot{\Upsilon}^{N})\bigg\}\geq-C_{0}^{\prime}>-\infty.

(3.27)

Therefore,
the uniform exponential integrability (
1.27
)
follows from (
3.15
), (
3.16
), and (
3.27
).

\bullet

Tightness:

Next, we prove
tightness of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
.
Although it follows from a slight modification of the argument in our previous work
[
54
, Subsection 6.2]
,
we present a proof here for readers’ convenience.

As a preliminary step,
we first prove that

Z_{N}
in (
1.26
) is uniformly bounded away from 0:

\displaystyle\inf_{N\in\mathbb{N}}Z_{N}>0.

(3.28)

In view of (
3.15
) and (
3.16
),
it suffices to establish an upper bound on
\mathcal{W}_{N}
in (
3.17
).
By Lemma
2.1
and (
3.19
), we have

\displaystyle\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}dx\bigg|^{3}

\displaystyle\lesssim\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{3}\|\Theta_{N}\|_{H^{\frac{1}{2}+2\varepsilon}}^{3}

\displaystyle\lesssim 1+\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{c}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{c}+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{c}.

Thus, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}&\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}\\
&\lesssim 1+\|:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-1-\varepsilon}}^{3}+\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{c}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{c}+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{c}.\end{split}

(3.29)

Then, from (
3.17
), Lemma
3.5
, and (
3.29
)
with Lemma
3.2
and (
3.25
),
we obtain

\displaystyle\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathcal{W}_{N}

\displaystyle\lesssim 1+\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\bigg(\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg)^{c}\Bigg]\lesssim 1

by taking
\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\equiv 0
, for example.
This proves (
3.28
).

We now prove tightness of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures.
Fix small
\varepsilon>0
and
let

B_{R}\subset H^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})

be the closed ball of radius
R>0
centered at the origin.
Then, by Rellich’s compactness lemma,
we see that
B_{R}
is compact in
H^{-\frac{1}{2}-2\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
.
In the following, we show that
given any small
\delta>0
, there exists
R=R(\delta)\gg 1

such that

\displaystyle\sup_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\rho_{N}(B_{R}^{c})<\delta.

(3.30)

Given
M\gg 1
,
let
F
be a bounded smooth non-negative function such that

\displaystyle F(u)=\begin{cases}M,&\text{if }\|u\|_{H^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}\leq\frac{R}{2},\\
0,&\text{if }\|u\|_{H^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}>R.\end{cases}

(3.31)

Then, from (
3.28
), we have

\displaystyle\rho_{N}(B_{R}^{c})\leq Z_{N}^{-1}\int e^{-F(u)-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)}d\mu\lesssim\int e^{-F(u)-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)}d\mu=:\widehat{Z}_{N},

(3.32)

uniformly in
N\gg 1
.
Under the change of variables (
3.12
)
(see also (
3.13
)),
define
\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})
by

\displaystyle\begin{split}\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})&=-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Y_{N}^{3}\!:dx-\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Theta_{N}^{2}dx-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Theta_{N}^{3}dx\\
&\hphantom{X}+A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3},\end{split}

(3.33)

where

\Theta_{N}=\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}

with
\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}=\pi_{N}\mathfrak{Z}_{N}
as in (
3.19
).
Then, by (
3.32
) and
the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}-\log\widehat{Z}_{N}=\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[&F(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})\\
&+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg].\end{split}

(3.34)

Since

Y+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\in\mathcal{H}_{\leq 2}
,
it follows from Lemma
3.2
, (
3.25
),
Chebyshev’s inequality,
and choosing
R\gg 1
that

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{P}\Big(&\|Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{H^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}>\tfrac{R}{2}\Big)\\
&\leq\mathbb{P}\Big(\|Y+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{H^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}>\tfrac{R}{4}\Big)+\mathbb{P}\Big(\|\Upsilon^{N}\|_{H^{1}}>\tfrac{R}{4}\Big)\\
&\leq\frac{1}{2}+\frac{16}{R^{2}}\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\Upsilon^{N}\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}\Big],\end{split}

(3.35)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
and
R\gg 1
.
Then,
from
(
3.31
), (
3.35
), and Lemma
3.2
,
we obtain

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\Big[F(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})\Big]&\geq M\mathbb{E}\Big[\mathbf{1}_{\big\{\|Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{H^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}\leq\tfrac{R}{2}\big\}}\Big]\\
&\geq\frac{M}{2}-\frac{16M}{R^{2}}\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\Upsilon^{N}\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}\Big]\\
&\geq\frac{M}{2}-\frac{1}{4}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg],\end{split}

(3.36)

where we set
M=\frac{1}{64}R^{2}
in the last step.
Hence, from (
3.34
), (
3.36
),
and repeating the computation leading to (
3.27
)
(by possibly making
\sigma_{0}
smaller), we obtain

\displaystyle\begin{split}-\log\widehat{Z}_{N}&\geq\frac{M}{2}+\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})+\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]\\
&\geq\frac{M}{4},\end{split}

(3.37)

uniformly
N\in\mathbb{N}
and
M=\frac{1}{64}R^{2}\gg 1
.
Therefore, given any small
\delta>0
, by choosing
R=R(\delta)\gg 1

and setting
M=\frac{1}{64}R^{2}\gg 1
,
the desired bound (
3.30
) follows from
(
3.32
) and (
3.37
).
This proves
tightness of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
.

We conclude this subsection by presenting the proofs of
Lemmas
3.5
and
3.6
.

Proof of Lemma
3.5
.

From (
2.5
), (
2.6
), (
2.4
), and (
2.3
)
in Lemma
2.1
followed by Young’s inequality,
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}&Y_{N}\Theta_{N}^{2}dx\bigg|\lesssim\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}\|\Theta_{N}\|_{H^{\frac{1}{2}+2\varepsilon}}\|\Theta_{N}\|_{L^{2}}\\
&\lesssim\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}\Big(\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{\frac{1}{2}+2\varepsilon}}\big(\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}\big)+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{2}\Big)\\
&\lesssim\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}\Big(\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}-2\varepsilon}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{\frac{1}{2}+2\varepsilon}\big(\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}\big)+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{2}\Big)\\
&\lesssim 1+C_{\delta}\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{c}+\delta\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+\delta\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{c},\end{split}

(3.38)

which yields (
3.20
).
As for
the second estimate (
3.21
),
it follows from Sobolev’s inequality, the interpolation (
2.3
),
and Young’s inequality that

\displaystyle\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}^{3}dx\bigg|\lesssim\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{3}\lesssim\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{\frac{3}{2}}\lesssim\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2},

(3.39)

while Hölder’s inequality with (
2.4
) shows

\displaystyle\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}dx\bigg|+\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}^{2}dx\bigg|+\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}^{3}dx\bigg|\lesssim 1+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{3}.

Note that, given any
\gamma>0
, there exists a constant
C=C(J)>0
such that

\displaystyle\bigg|\sum_{j=1}^{J}a_{j}\bigg|^{\gamma}\geq\frac{1}{2}|a_{1}|^{\gamma}-C\bigg(\sum_{j=2}^{J}|a_{j}|^{\gamma}\bigg)

(3.40)

for any
a_{j}\in\mathbb{R}
. See Section 5 in
[
54
]
.
Then, from (
3.40
) and Cauchy’s inequality,
we have

\displaystyle A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}

\displaystyle\geq\frac{A}{2}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(2Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}-CA\Bigg\{\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:dx\bigg|^{3}+|\sigma|^{3}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}dx\bigg|^{3}

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXX}+|\sigma|^{3}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}dx\bigg|^{3}+\sigma^{6}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}^{2}dx\bigg|^{3}\Bigg\}

\displaystyle\geq\frac{A}{2}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(2Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}-\delta\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXX}-C_{\delta,\sigma}\Bigg\{\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:dx\bigg|^{3}+\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{6}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{6}\Bigg\}.

This proves (
3.22
).
This completes the proof of Lemma
3.5
.
∎

Next, we present the proof of
Lemma
3.6
.

Proof of Lemma
3.6
.

If we have

\displaystyle\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\gg\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}dx\bigg|,

(3.41)

then, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}=\bigg(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}^{2}dx\bigg)^{3}\sim\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(2Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3},\end{split}

(3.42)

which shows (
3.23
).
Hence, we assume that

\displaystyle\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}dx\bigg|

(3.43)

in the following.

Given
j\in\mathbb{N}
,
define the sharp frequency projections
\Pi_{j}

with a Fourier multiplier

\mathbf{1}_{\{|n|\leq 2\}}
when
j=1

and
\mathbf{1}_{\{2^{j-1}<|n|\leq 2^{j}\}}
when
j\geq 2
.
We also set
\Pi_{\leq j}=\sum_{k=1}^{j}\Pi_{k}

and
\Pi_{>j}=\Id-\Pi_{\leq j}
.
Then,
write
\Upsilon_{N}
as

\displaystyle\Upsilon_{N}=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\Pi_{j}\Upsilon_{N}=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(\lambda_{j}\Pi_{j}Y_{N}+w_{j}),

(3.44)

where
\lambda_{j}
and
w_{j}
are given by

\displaystyle\lambda_{j}

\displaystyle:=\begin{cases}\frac{\langle\Upsilon_{N},\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\rangle}{\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}},&\text{if }\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}\neq 0,\\
0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\text{and}\qquad w_{j}:=\Pi_{j}\Upsilon_{N}-\lambda_{j}\Pi_{j}Y_{N}.

(3.45)

By definition,
w_{j}=\Pi_{j}w_{j}
is orthogonal to
\Pi_{j}Y_{N}
(and also to
Y_{N}
) in
L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
.
Thus, we have

\displaystyle\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}

\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\Big(\lambda_{j}^{2}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|w_{j}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big),

(3.46)

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}dx

\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

(3.47)

Hence,
from (
3.43
), (
3.46
), and (
3.47
), we have

\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}^{2}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\lesssim\bigg|\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg|.

(3.48)

Fix
j_{0}=j_{0}(\omega)\in\mathbb{N}
(to be chosen later).
By Cauchy-Schwarz’s inequality and (
3.45
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg|\sum_{j=j_{0}+1}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg|&\leq\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}^{2}2^{2j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigg(\sum_{j=j_{0}+1}^{\infty}2^{-2j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
&\leq\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}2^{2j}\|\Pi_{j}\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigg(\sum_{j=j_{0}+1}^{\infty}2^{-2j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
&\sim\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}\|\Pi_{>j_{0}}Y_{N}\|_{H^{-1}}.\end{split}

(3.49)

On the other hand, it follows
from
Cauchy-Schwarz’s inequality,
(
3.48
), and
Cauchy’s inequality that

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg|\sum_{j=1}^{j_{0}}\lambda_{j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg|&\leq\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}^{2}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{j_{0}}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
&\leq C\bigg|\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg|^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{j_{0}}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
&\leq\frac{1}{2}\bigg|\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg|+C^{\prime}\|\Pi_{\leq j_{0}}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.\end{split}

(3.50)

Hence, from (
3.49
) and (
3.50
),
we obtain

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg|\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg|\lesssim\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}\|\Pi_{>j_{0}}Y_{N}\|_{H^{-1}}+\|\Pi_{\leq j_{0}}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.\end{split}

(3.51)

Since
Y_{N}
is spatially homogeneous, we have

\displaystyle\|\Pi_{>j_{0}}Y_{N}\|_{H^{-1}}^{2}

\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}\Pi_{>j_{0}}Y_{N})^{2}\!:dx+\mathbb{E}\big[(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}\Pi_{>j_{0}}Y_{N})^{2}\big].

(3.52)

Recalling (
3.2
),
we can bound
the second term by

\displaystyle\widetilde{\sigma}_{j_{0}}:=\mathbb{E}\big[(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}\Pi_{>j_{0}}Y_{N})^{2}\big]=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\\
|n|>2^{j_{0}}\end{subarray}}\frac{\chi_{N}^{2}(n)}{\langle n\rangle^{4}}\lesssim 2^{-j_{0}}.

(3.53)

Let
Z_{N,j_{0}}=\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}\Pi_{>j_{0}}Y_{N}
.
Proceeding as in the proof of Lemma 2.5 in
[
63
]

with Lemma
2.6
, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\bigg(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Z_{N,j_{0}}^{2}\!:dx\bigg)^{2}\Bigg]&=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}_{x}\times\mathbb{T}^{3}_{y}}\mathbb{E}\Big[H_{2}(Z_{N,j_{0}}(x);\widetilde{\sigma}_{j_{0}})H_{2}(Z_{N,j_{0}}(y);\widetilde{\sigma}_{j_{0}})\Big]dxdy\\
&=2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\\
|n_{j}|>2^{j_{0}}\end{subarray}}\frac{\chi_{N}^{2}(n_{1})\chi_{N}^{2}(n_{2})}{\langle n_{1}\rangle^{4}\langle n_{2}\rangle^{4}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}_{x}\times\mathbb{T}^{3}_{y}}e_{n_{1}+n_{2}}(x-y)dxdy\\
&=2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\\
|n|>2^{j_{0}}\end{subarray}}\frac{\chi_{N}^{4}(n)}{\langle n\rangle^{8}}\sim 2^{-5j_{0}}.\end{split}

(3.54)

Now, define a non-negative random variable
B_{1}(\omega)
by

\displaystyle B_{1}(\omega)=\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}2^{4j}\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Z_{N,j}^{2}\!:dx\Big)^{2}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}.

(3.55)

By Minkowski’s integral inequality, the Wiener chaos estimate (Lemma
2.5
), and (
3.54
),
we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[B_{1}^{p}\big]\leq p^{p}\Bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}2^{4j}\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!Z_{N,j}^{2}\!:dx\bigg\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\Bigg)^{\frac{p}{2}}\lesssim p^{p}<\infty

(3.56)

for any finite
p\geq 2
(and hence for any finite
p\geq 1
).
Hence, from
(
3.52
), (
3.53
), and (
3.55
), we obtain

\displaystyle\|\Pi_{>j_{0}}Y_{N}\|_{H^{-1}}^{2}\lesssim 2^{-2j_{0}}B_{1}(\omega)+2^{-j_{0}}.

(3.57)

Next, define a non-negative random variable
B_{2}(\omega)
by

B_{2}(\omega)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!(\prod_{j}Y_{N})^{2}\!:dx\bigg|.

Then, a similar computation shows

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\Pi_{\leq j_{0}}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}&=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!(\Pi_{\leq j_{0}}Y_{N})^{2}\!:dx+\mathbb{E}\big[(\Pi_{\leq j_{0}}Y_{N})^{2}\big]\\
&\lesssim B_{2}(\omega)+2^{j_{0}}\end{split}

(3.58)

and
\mathbb{E}\big[B_{2}^{p}\big]\leq C_{p}<\infty

for any finite
p\geq 1
.

Therefore, putting
(
3.43
), (
3.47
)
(
3.51
), (
3.57
), and (
3.58
)
together,
choosing
2^{j_{0}}\sim 1+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{\frac{2}{3}}
,
and applying Cauchy’s inequality,
we obtain

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}&\lesssim\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}dx\bigg|^{3}=\bigg|\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}\|\Pi_{j}Y_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\bigg|^{3}\\
&\lesssim\Big(2^{-3j_{0}}B_{1}(\omega)^{\frac{3}{2}}+2^{-\frac{3}{2}j_{0}}\Big)\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{3}+B_{2}^{3}(\omega)+2^{3j_{0}}\\
&\lesssim\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+B_{1}^{3}(\omega)+B_{2}^{3}(\omega)+1.\end{split}

(3.59)

This proves (
3.23
) in the case (
3.43
) holds.
This concludes the proof of Lemma
3.6
.
∎

Remark 3.7
.

From the proof of Lemma
3.6

(see (
3.41
) and (
3.59
))
with Lemma
3.6
,
we also have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N}dx\bigg|^{3}\Bigg]&\lesssim\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\Big]+1\\
&\lesssim\mathcal{U}_{N}+1,\end{split}

(3.60)

where
\mathcal{U}_{N}
is as in (
3.24
).

3.3.
Uniqueness of the limiting
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure

The tightness of the truncated Gibbs measures
\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
, proven in the previous subsection,
together with Prokhorov’s theorem implies
existence of a weakly convergent subsequence.
In this subsection, we prove uniqueness of
the limiting
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure, which allows us to conclude
the weak convergence of the entire sequence

\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
.
While we follow the uniqueness argument in our previous work
[
54
, Subsection 6.3]
,
there are extra terms to control due to the focusing nature of the problem under consideration.

Proposition 3.8
.

Let
\{\rho_{N^{1}_{k}}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}

and
\{\rho_{N^{2}_{k}}\}_{k=1}^{\infty}
be
two weakly convergent subsequences
of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures

\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
defined in (
1.25
),
converging weakly to
\rho^{(1)}
and
\rho^{(2)}
as
k\to\infty
, respectively.
Then, we have

\rho^{(1)}=\rho^{(2)}
.

Proof.

\bullet

Step 1:

We first show that

\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}Z_{N^{1}_{k}}=\lim_{k\to\infty}Z_{N^{2}_{k}},

(3.61)

where
Z_{N}
is as in (
1.26
).
By taking a further subsequence, we may assume that

N^{1}_{k}\geq N^{2}_{k}
,
k\in\mathbb{N}
.
Recall the change of variables (
3.12
)
and
let
\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})
be as in (
3.33
).
Then, by
the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
), we have

\displaystyle-\log Z_{N^{j}_{k}}=\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N^{j}_{k}}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{j}_{k}}(Y+\Upsilon^{N^{j}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{j}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N^{j}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]

(3.62)

for
j=1,2
and
k\in\mathbb{N}
.
We point out that
Y
and
\mathfrak{Z}_{N}
do not depend
on the drift
\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}

in (
3.62
).

Given
\delta>0
,
let
{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}
be an almost optimizer for (
3.62
) with
j=2
:

\displaystyle-\log Z_{N^{2}_{k}}

\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{2}_{k}}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]-\delta.

(3.63)

By setting
{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}:=\pi_{N^{2}_{k}}{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}
, we have

\displaystyle\pi_{N^{1}_{k}}{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}={\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}

(3.64)

since
N^{1}_{k}\geq N^{2}_{k}
.
Then, by choosing

\Upsilon^{N^{1}_{k}}={\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}
,
it follows from (
3.63
) and (
3.64
) that

\displaystyle-

\displaystyle\log Z_{N^{1}_{k}}+\log Z_{N^{2}_{k}}

\displaystyle\leq\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N^{1}_{k}}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{1}_{k}}(Y+\Upsilon^{N^{1}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{1}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N^{1}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]

\displaystyle\quad\quad-\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{2}_{k}}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]+\delta

\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{1}_{k}}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{1}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]

\displaystyle\quad\quad-\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{2}_{k}}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]+\delta

\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\Big[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}(Y_{N^{1}_{k}}+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{1}_{k}})-\widehat{R}^{\diamond}(Y_{N^{2}_{k}}+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{2}_{k}})\Big]+\delta,

(3.65)

where
\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{j}_{k}}=\pi_{N^{j}_{k}}\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{j}_{k}}
is as in (
3.19
).
Here,

\widehat{R}^{\diamond}
is defined by

\displaystyle\begin{split}\widehat{R}^{\diamond}(Y+\Upsilon+\sigma\mathfrak{Z})&=-\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y\Theta^{2}dx-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Theta^{3}dx\\
&\hphantom{X}+A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y^{2}\!:+2Y\Theta+\Theta^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3},\end{split}

where

.

We now estimate the right-hand side of (

).
The main point is that in the difference

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}(Y_{N^{1}_{k}}+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{1}_{k}})-\widehat{R}^{\diamond}(Y_{N^{2}_{k}}+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{2}_{k}})\Big],

we only have differences in

which allows us to gain a negative power of

The contribution from

\displaystyle\begin{split}-\sigma\mathbb{E}&\bigg[\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(Y_{N^{1}_{k}}-Y_{N^{2}_{k}}){\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}^{2}dx\bigg]\\
&-\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(Y_{N^{1}_{k}}-Y_{N^{2}_{k}})(2{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{1}_{k}})\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{1}_{k}}dx\bigg]\\
&-\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N^{2}_{k}}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{1}_{k}}-\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{2}_{k}})(2{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{1}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{2}_{k}})dx\bigg].\end{split}

(3.68)

Let
\mathcal{U}_{N_{k}^{2}}=\mathcal{U}_{N_{k}^{2}}(\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N_{k}^{2}})

) with

and

.
Then, from Lemmas
3.2

, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}\Big]\lesssim 1+\mathcal{U}_{N_{k}^{2}}.

Now, proceeding as in (
3.38
)
together with Hölder’s inequality in
\omega

and Young’s inequality,
we bound
the first term in (

) by

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{E}&\Big[\|Y_{N^{1}_{k}}-Y_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{L^{2}}^{\frac{3}{2}-2\varepsilon}\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{H^{1}}^{\frac{1}{2}+2\varepsilon}\Big]\\
&\leq\|Y_{N^{1}_{k}}-Y_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{L^{\frac{6}{3-4\varepsilon}}_{\omega}\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}_{x}}\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}L^{2}_{x}}^{\frac{3}{2}-2\varepsilon}\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{L^{2}_{\omega}H^{1}_{x}}^{\frac{1}{2}+2\varepsilon}\\
&\lesssim(N^{2}_{k})^{-a}\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}L^{2}_{x}}^{\frac{3}{2}-2\varepsilon}\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{L^{2}_{\omega}H^{1}_{x}}^{\frac{1}{2}+2\varepsilon}\\
&\lesssim(N^{2}_{k})^{-a}\Big(1+\mathcal{U}_{N_{k}^{2}}\Big),\end{split}

(3.69)

where the second inequality follows from
a modification of the proof of Lemma
3.2
(i)
and noting that the Fourier transform of

Y_{N^{1}_{k}}-Y_{N^{2}_{k}}
is supported on the frequencies
\{|n|\gtrsim N^{2}_{k}\}
,
which allows us to gain a small negative power of
N^{2}_{k}
.
Note that

However, the sizes of

The same comment applies to Subsections

The second and third terms in (

)
to control the

-terms).
As a result, we can bound the first two terms on the right-hand side of (

)

\displaystyle\begin{split}(N^{2}_{k})^{-a}\Big(&C(Y_{N^{1}_{k}},Y_{N^{2}_{k}},\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{1}_{k}},\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})+\mathcal{U}_{N_{k}^{2}}\Big)\lesssim(N^{2}_{k})^{-a}\Big(1+\mathcal{U}_{N_{k}^{2}}\Big)\end{split}

(3.70)

for some small

,
where

and

,

,

, in view of Lemma
3.2

It remains to treat the difference coming from the last term in (

By Young’s and Hölder’s inequalities, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N_{k}^{1}}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N_{k}^{1}}({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}})+({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}})^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}

\displaystyle\hphantom{XX}-\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N_{k}^{2}}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N_{k}^{2}}({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{2}})+({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{2}})^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}\bigg]

\displaystyle\lesssim\Bigg\{\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N_{k}^{1}}^{2}\!:-:\!Y_{N_{k}^{2}}^{2}\!:\Big)dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}+\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(Y_{N_{k}^{1}}-Y_{N_{k}^{2}}){\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}

\displaystyle\hphantom{XX}+\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(Y_{N_{k}^{1}}-Y_{N_{k}^{2}})\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}}dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}+\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N_{k}^{2}}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}}-\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{2}})dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}

\displaystyle\quad\times\Bigg\{\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N_{k}^{1}}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N_{k}^{1}}({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}})+({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}})^{2}\Big)dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}^{2}

\displaystyle\hphantom{XX}+\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N_{k}^{2}}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N_{k}^{2}}({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{2}})+({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{2}})^{2}\Big)dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}^{2}\Bigg\}

\displaystyle=:\hskip 0.56905pt\textup{I}\hskip 0.56905pt\times\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}.

We divide

\displaystyle\begin{split}\hskip 0.56905pt\textup{I}\hskip 0.56905pt&=\Bigg(\hskip 0.56905pt\textup{I}\hskip 0.56905pt-\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(Y_{N_{k}^{1}}-Y_{N_{k}^{2}}){\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}\Bigg)+\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(Y_{N_{k}^{1}}-Y_{N_{k}^{2}}){\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}\\

(3.72)

By the definition (

)

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(Y_{N_{k}^{1}}-Y_{N_{k}^{2}}){\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}dx\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\pi_{N^{2}_{k}}(Y_{N_{k}^{1}}-Y_{N_{k}^{2}})\cdot{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}dx=0

By

\displaystyle\begin{split}\hskip 0.56905pt\textup{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{1}&\lesssim\|:\!Y_{N_{k}^{1}}^{2}\!:-:\!Y_{N_{k}^{2}}^{2}\!:\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}\mathcal{C}^{-1-\varepsilon}_{x}}\\
&\hphantom{X}+\|Y_{N_{k}^{1}}-Y_{N_{k}^{2}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}_{x}}\|\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}_{x}}+\|Y_{N_{k}^{2}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}_{x}}\|\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}}-\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{2}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}_{x}}\\
&\hphantom{X}+\|\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}}-\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{2}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}_{x}}\Big(\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}L^{2}_{x}}+\|\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{1}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}_{x}}+\|\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{2}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}_{x}}\Big)\\
&\lesssim(N_{k}^{2})^{-a}\Big(1+\mathcal{U}_{N_{k}^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{1}{6}},\end{split}

(3.74)

where we used Lemma
3.2
and (
3.25
)
in bounding the terms involving
Y_{N_{k}^{j}}
and
\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{j}}=\pi_{N_{k}^{j}}\mathfrak{Z}_{N_{k}^{j}}
.
As for
I I
in (
3.71
),
it follows from (
3.60
), Lemma
3.6
, and (
3.24
) that

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg\|&\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N_{k}^{j}}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N_{k}^{j}}({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{j}})+({\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N_{k}^{j}})^{2}\Big)dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}\\
&\lesssim 1+\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N_{k}^{j}}{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}dx\bigg\|_{L^{3}_{\omega}}+\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N_{k}^{2}}\|_{L^{6}_{\omega}L^{2}_{x}}^{2}\\
&\lesssim 1+\mathcal{U}_{N_{k}^{2}}^{\frac{1}{3}}.\end{split}

(3.75)

From
(
3.26
),
(
3.16
), (
3.17
),
(
3.33
),
and replacing
{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}
by 0 in view of
(
3.62
),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\,\mathcal{U}_{N_{k}^{2}}(\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}})&\leq 10C_{0}^{\prime}+10\sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{2}_{k}}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]\\
&\lesssim 1+\delta+\sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{E}\big[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{2}_{k}}(Y+0+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})\big]\\
&\lesssim 1.\end{split}

(3.76)

Hence,
from (
3.73
), (
3.74
), (
3.75
),
and (
3.76
), we obtain that

\displaystyle\hskip 0.56905pt\textup{I}\hskip 0.56905pt\cdot\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}\lesssim(N^{2}_{k})^{-a}\longrightarrow 0,

(3.77)

as

.
Therefore, from (
3.70
) and (
3.77
),
we conclude
that

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}(Y_{N^{1}_{k}}+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{1}_{k}})-\widehat{R}^{\diamond}(Y_{N^{2}_{k}}+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{2}_{k}})\bigg]\longrightarrow 0,

(3.78)

as
k\to\infty
.
Since the choice of

was arbitrary,
it follows from (
3.65
) and (

) that

\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}Z_{N^{1}_{k}}\geq\lim_{k\to\infty}Z_{N^{2}_{k}}.

(3.79)

By taking a subsequence of
\{N^{2}_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
,
still denoted by
\{N^{2}_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
,
we may assume that
N^{1}_{k}\leq N^{2}_{k}
.
By repeating the computation above,
we then obtain

\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}Z_{N^{1}_{k}}\leq\lim_{k\to\infty}Z_{N^{2}_{k}}.

(3.80)

Therefore,
(
3.61
) follows from (
3.79
) and (
3.80
).

\bullet

Step 2:

Next, we prove
\rho^{(1)}=\rho^{(2)}
.
This claim follows from a small modification of Step 1.
For this purpose, we need to prove that for every bounded Lipschitz continuous function
F:\mathcal{C}^{-100}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\to\mathbb{R}
,
we have

\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}\int\exp(F(u))d\rho_{N^{1}_{k}}\geq\lim_{k\to\infty}\int\exp(F(u))d\rho_{N^{2}_{k}}

under the condition
N^{1}_{k}\geq N^{2}_{k}
,
k\in\mathbb{N}

(which can be always satisfied by taking a subsequence of
\{N^{1}_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
).
In view of (
1.26
) and (
3.61
), it suffices to show

\displaystyle\begin{split}\limsup_{k\to\infty}\bigg[-\log\Big(\int&\exp(F(u)-R_{N^{1}_{k}}^{\diamond}(u))d\mu\Big)\\
&+\log\Big(\int\exp(F(u)-R_{N^{2}_{k}}^{\diamond}(u))d\mu\Big)\bigg]\leq 0.\end{split}

(3.81)

By the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}-&\log\Big(\int\exp(F(u)-R_{N^{j}_{k}}^{\diamond}(u))d\mu\Big)\\
&=\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N^{j}_{k}}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-F(Y+\Upsilon^{N^{j}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{j}_{k}})\\
&\hphantom{XXXXXXXX}+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{j}_{k}}(Y+\Upsilon^{N^{j}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{j}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N^{j}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg],\end{split}

(3.82)

where
\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{j}_{k}}(Y+\Upsilon^{N^{j}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{j}_{k}})
is as in (
3.33
).
Given
\delta>0
,
let
{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}
be an almost optimizer for (
3.82
) with
j=2
:

\displaystyle-\log

\displaystyle\Big(\int\exp(F(u)-R_{N^{2}_{k}}^{\diamond}(u))d\mu\Big)

\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\bigg[-F(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})

\displaystyle\quad+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{2}_{k}}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]-\delta.

Then, by choosing
\Upsilon^{N^{1}_{k}}={\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}=\pi_{N^{2}_{k}}{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}

and proceeding as in (
3.65
),
we have

\displaystyle-

\displaystyle\log\Big(\int\exp(F(u)-R_{N^{1}_{k}}^{\diamond}(u))d\mu\Big)+\log\Big(\int\exp(F(u)-R_{N^{2}_{k}}^{\diamond}(u))d\mu\Big)

\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\bigg[-F(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{1}_{k}})

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXi}+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{1}_{k}}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{1}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]

\displaystyle\quad-\mathbb{E}\bigg[-F(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXi}+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N^{2}_{k}}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]+\delta

\displaystyle\leq\Lip(F)\cdot\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\pi_{N^{2}_{k}}^{\perp}{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}-\sigma(\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{1}_{k}}-\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-100}}\Big]

\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}\Big[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}(Y_{N^{1}_{k}}+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{1}_{k}})-\widehat{R}^{\diamond}(Y_{N^{2}_{k}}+{\underline{\Upsilon}}_{N^{2}_{k}}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N^{2}_{k}})\Big]+\delta,

(3.83)

where
\pi_{N}^{\perp}=\text{Id}-\pi_{N}
and
\widehat{R}^{\diamond}
is as in (
3.66
).
We can proceed as in Step 1 to show that the second term
on the right-hand side of (
3.83
)
satisfies (
3.78
).
Here, we need to use the boundedness of
F
in showing an analogue
of (
3.76
) in the current context
(with an almost optimizer

{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}
for (
3.82
)).

Finally, we estimate the first term on the right-hand side of (
3.83
).
Write

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[

\displaystyle\|\pi_{N^{2}_{k}}^{\perp}{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}-\sigma(\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{1}_{k}}-\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}})\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-100}}\Big]

\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\pi_{N^{2}_{k}}^{\perp}\Upsilon^{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-100}}\Big]+\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{1}_{k}}-\mathfrak{Z}_{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-100}}\Big].

A standard computation
with (
3.11
)
shows that the second term on the right-hand side tends
to 0 as
k\to\infty
.
As for the first term,
from Lemma
3.2
and (an analogue of) (
3.76
), we obtain

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\pi_{N^{2}_{k}}^{\perp}{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-100}}\Big]\lesssim(N^{2}_{k})^{-a}\|{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}}\|_{L^{2}_{\omega}H^{1}_{x}}\lesssim(N^{2}_{k})^{-a}\Big(\sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\,\mathcal{U}_{N^{2}_{k}}\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\longrightarrow 0,

as
k\to\infty
.
Since the choice of
\delta>0
was arbitrary,
we conclude (
3.81
)
and hence
\rho^{(1)}=\rho^{(2)}
.
This completes the proof of Proposition
3.8
.
∎

Remark 3.9
.

In the proof of Proposition
3.8
,
we used the orthogonality relation (
3.73
)
to conclude that
\hskip 0.56905pt\textup{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{2}=0
.
While the same orthogonality holds
for the ball frequency projector
\pi_{N}^{\text{ball}}
in (
1.41
),
such an orthogonality relation is false for the smooth
frequency projector
\pi_{N}^{\text{smooth}}
in (
1.42
).
As seen from the proof of Lemma
3.6

and the uniform bound (
3.76
)
on
\mathcal{U}_{N^{2}_{k}}(\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N^{2}_{k}})
, the quantity

\hskip 0.56905pt\textup{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{2}
in (
3.72
) is critical (with respect to the spatial regularity/integrability and
also with respect to the
\omega
-integrability).
From Remark
3.7

and (
3.76
), we see that the quantity
\hskip 0.56905pt\textup{I}\hskip 0.56905pt_{2}
is bounded,
uniformly in
k\in\mathbb{N}
.
In the absence of the orthogonality (
3.73
), however, we do
not know how to show that this term tends to
0
as
k\to\infty

in the case of the smooth
frequency projector
\pi_{N}^{\text{smooth}}
.
We point out that the same issue also appears in
the proofs of
Propositions
4.1

and
6.10

in the case of the smooth
frequency projector
\pi_{N}^{\text{smooth}}
.

3.4.
Singularity of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure

We conclude this section
by proving mutual singularity of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
\rho
,
constructed in the previous subsections,
and the base Gaussian free field
\mu
in (
1.16
).
In Section 4 of
[
4
]
,
Barashkov and Gubinelli proved the singularity of the
\Phi^{4}_{3}
-measure
by making use of the shifted measure.
In the following, we
follow our previous work
[
54
]

and present a direct proof of
singularity of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
without referring to a shifted measure.
See also Appendix
A
, where we construct
a shifted measure with respect to which the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
is absolutely continuous.

Proposition 3.10
.

Let
R_{N}
be as in (
1.23
) with
\gamma=3
,
and
\varepsilon>0
.
Then,
there exists a strictly increasing sequence
\{N_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathbb{N}
such that
the set

\displaystyle S:=\big\{u\in H^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3}):\lim_{k\to\infty}(\log N_{k})^{-\frac{3}{4}}R_{N_{k}}(u)=0\big\}

satisfies

\displaystyle\mu(S)=1\qquad\text{but}\qquad\rho(S)=0.

(3.84)

In particular, the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
\rho
and
the massive Gaussian free field
\mu
in (
1.16
) are mutually singular.

Proof.

From (
1.23
) with
\gamma=3
, the Wiener chaos estimate (Lemma
2.5
),
Lemma
2.6
,
and Lemma
2.4
,
we have

\displaystyle\|R_{N}(u)\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}^{2}

\displaystyle\lesssim\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!u_{N}^{3}\!:dx\bigg\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}^{2}+\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!u_{N}^{2}\!:dx\bigg\|_{L^{6}(\mu)}^{6}

\displaystyle\lesssim\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!u_{N}^{3}\!:dx\bigg\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}^{2}+\bigg\|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!u_{N}^{2}\!:dx\bigg\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}^{6}

\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1}+n_{2}+n_{3}=0\\
n_{j}\in NQ\end{subarray}}\langle n_{1}\rangle^{-2}\langle n_{2}\rangle^{-2}\langle n_{3}\rangle^{-2}+\bigg(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1}+n_{2}=0\\
n_{j}\in NQ\end{subarray}}\langle n_{1}\rangle^{-2}\langle n_{2}\rangle^{-2}\bigg)^{3}

\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|n_{1}|,|n-n_{1}|\lesssim N\end{subarray}}\langle n_{1}\rangle^{-2}\langle n-n_{1}\rangle^{-1}+1

\displaystyle\lesssim\log N,

where

Q
denotes the cube of side length
2
in
\mathbb{R}^{3}
centered at the origin
as in (
1.21
).
Thus, we have

\lim_{N\to\infty}(\log N)^{-\frac{3}{4}}\|R_{N}(u)\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}\lesssim\lim_{N\to\infty}(\log N)^{-\frac{1}{4}}=0.

Hence, there exists a subsequence such that

\lim_{k\to\infty}(\log N_{k})^{-\frac{3}{4}}R_{N_{k}}(u)=0,

almost surely with respect to
\mu
.
This proves
\mu(S)=1
in (

).

Given
k\in\mathbb{N}
, define
G_{k}(u)
by

\displaystyle G_{k}(u)=(\log N_{k})^{-\frac{3}{4}}R_{N_{k}}(u).

(3.85)

In the following,

tends to

in

.
This will imply that there exists a subsequence
of

,
almost surely with respect to the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
\rho
,
which in turn yields the second claim in (

):

\rho(S)=0
.

Let

be a smooth bump function as in Subsection

.
By Fatou’s lemma, the weak convergence of

to

,
the boundedness of

\displaystyle\begin{split}\int e^{G_{k}(u)}d\rho(u)&\leq\liminf_{K\to\infty}\int\phi\bigg(\frac{G_{k}(u)}{K}\bigg)e^{G_{k}(u)}d\rho(u)\\
&=\liminf_{K\to\infty}\lim_{M\to\infty}\int\phi\bigg(\frac{G_{k}(u)}{K}\bigg)e^{G_{k}(u)}d\rho_{M}(u)\\
&\leq\lim_{M\to\infty}\int e^{G_{k}(u)}d\rho_{M}(u)=Z^{-1}\lim_{M\to\infty}\int e^{G_{k}(u)-R_{M}^{\diamond}(u)}d\mu(u)\\
&=:Z^{-1}\lim_{M\to\infty}C_{M,k},\end{split}

provided that

Our main goal is to show that the right-hand side of (

As in the previous subsections, we proceed with

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} -\log C_{M,k}&=\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{M}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-(\log N_{k})^{-\frac{3}{4}}R_{N_{k}}(Y+\Upsilon^{M}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M})\\

Lemma 3.11
.

We have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{0}^{1}\langle\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}(t),\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{M}(t)\rangle_{H^{1}_{x}}dt\bigg]\sim\log N

By (

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \sigma\mathbb{E}&\bigg[\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\!:\!Y^{2}_{N_{k}}\!:\Theta_{N_{k}}dx\bigg]=\sigma\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\!:\!Y_{N_{k}}^{2}(t)\!:\dot{\Theta}_{N_{k}}(t)dt\bigg]\\

(3.97)

Proof of Lemma

.

For simplicity, we suppress the time dependence in the following.
From (

), we have

\displaystyle\widehat{\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}}_{N}(n)

\displaystyle=\langle n\rangle^{-2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\\

(3.100)

for

On the other hand, when

that

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[|\widehat{\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}}_{N}(0)|^{2}\Big]=\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n_{1}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\\
n_{1}\in NQ\end{subarray}}\big(|\widehat{Y}_{N}(n_{1})|^{2}-\langle n_{1}\rangle^{-2}\big)\Big)^{2}\bigg]\lesssim\sum_{n_{1}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\langle n_{1}\rangle^{-4}\lesssim 1,

(3.101)

where
Q
is as in (
1.21
).
Hence, from (
3.100
) and (
3.101
),
we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{0}^{1}

\displaystyle\langle\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}(t),\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{M}(t)\rangle_{H^{1}_{x}}dt\bigg]=\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\langle n\rangle^{2}\widehat{\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}}_{N}(n,t)\overline{\widehat{\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}}_{M}(n,t)}\bigg]dt

\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\setminus\{0\}}\langle n\rangle^{2}\widehat{\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}}_{N}(n,t)\overline{\widehat{\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}}_{M}(n,t)}\bigg]dt+O(1).

We now proceed as in the proof

) in Lemma

By applying (

) and Lemma

,
and summing over

and
|n_{j}|\leq N
,

we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}

\displaystyle\Bigg[\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}\setminus\{0\}}\langle n\rangle^{2}\widehat{\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}}_{N}(n,t)\overline{\widehat{\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}}_{M}(n,t)}\bigg]

\displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{\chi_{N}(n)\chi_{M}(n)}{\langle n\rangle^{2}}

\displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{t^{2}\chi_{N}(n)\chi_{M}(n)}{\langle n\rangle^{2}}\sum_{n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{\chi_{N}^{2}(n_{1})\chi_{N}^{2}(n_{2})}{\langle n_{1}\rangle^{2}\langle n_{2}\rangle^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}_{x}\times\mathbb{T}^{3}_{y}}e_{n_{1}+n_{2}-n}(x-y)dxdy

where

4.
Non-normalizability in the strongly nonlinear regime

4.1.
Reference measures and the
\sigma
-finite
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure

In this section, we prove non-normalizability
of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure in the strongly nonlinear regime
(Theorem
1.8
(ii)).
In
[
54
]
,
we introduced a strategy for establishing
non-normalizability
in the context of the focusing Hartree
\Phi^{4}_{3}
-measures on
\mathbb{T}^{3}
, using the
Boué-Dupuis variational formula.
We point out that, in
[
54
]
,
the focusing Hartree
\Phi^{4}_{3}
-measures
were absolutely continuous with respect to the base Gaussian free field
\mu
.
Moreover, the truncated potential energy
R_{N}^{\text{Hartree}}(u)
and the
corresponding density

e^{-R_{N}^{\text{Hartree}}(u)}

of the truncated focusing Hartree
\Phi^{4}_{3}
-measures
formed convergent sequences.
In
[
54
]
, we proved the following version of the non-normalizability
of the focusing Hartree
\Phi^{4}_{3}
-measure:

\displaystyle\sup_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\Big[e^{-R_{N}^{\text{Hartree}}(u)}\Big]=\infty.

(4.1)

Denoting the limiting density by
e^{-R^{\text{Hartree}}(u)}
,
this result says that the
\sigma
-finite version of the focusing Hartree
\Phi^{4}_{3}
-measure:

e^{-R^{\text{Hartree}}(u)}d\mu(u)

is not normalizable (i.e. there is no normalization constant
to make this into a probability measure).
See also
[
61
]
for an analogous non-normalizability result
for the log-correlated focusing Gibbs measures with a quartic interaction potential.

The main new difficulty in our current problem
is the singularity of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure.
In particular, the potential energy
R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)
in (
1.24
)
(and the corresponding density
e^{-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)}
)
does
not
converge to any limit.
Hence, even if we prove a non-normalizability statement
of the form (
4.1
),
it might still be possible that
by choosing a sequence of constants
\widehat{Z}_{N}
appropriately,
the measure
\widehat{Z}_{N}^{-1}e^{-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)}d\mu
has a weak limit.
This is precisely the case for the
\Phi^{4}_{3}
-measure;
see
[
3
]
.
The non-convergence claim in Theorem
1.8
(ii)
for the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures (see Proposition
4.4
below)
tells us that this is not the case for the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure.

In order to overcome this issue,
we first construct a reference measure
\nu_{\delta}

as a weak limit of the following tamed version of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
(with
\delta>0
):

\displaystyle d\nu_{N,\delta}(u)=Z_{N,\delta}^{-1}\exp\Big(-\delta F(\pi_{N}u)-R^{\diamond}_{N}(u)\Big)d\mu(u)

for some appropriate taming function
F
; see (
4.6
).
See Proposition
4.1
.
We also show that
F(u)
, without the frequency projection
\pi_{N}
on
u
, is well defined almost surely
with respect to the limiting reference measure
\nu_{\delta}=\lim_{N\to\infty}\nu_{N,\delta}
.
This allows us to construct a
\sigma
-finite version of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure:

\displaystyle d\overline{\rho}_{\delta}=e^{\delta F(u)}d\nu_{\delta}=\lim_{N\to\infty}Z_{N,\delta}^{-1}\,e^{\delta F(u)}e^{-\delta F(\pi_{N}u)-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)}d\mu(u).

(4.2)

The main point is that while the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
\rho_{N}

(=
\nu_{N,\delta}
with
\delta=0
) may not be convergent,
the tamed version
\nu_{N,\delta}
of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
converges to the limit
\nu_{\delta}
, thus allowing us to define
a
\sigma
-finite version of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure.
We then show that this
\sigma
-finite version
\overline{\rho}_{\delta}

of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure in (
4.2
) is not normalizable
in the strongly nonlinear regime.
See Proposition
4.2
.
Furthermore, as a corollary to this non-normalizability
result of the
\sigma
-finite version
\overline{\rho}_{\delta}

of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure,
we also show that
the sequence
\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}

of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures defined in (
1.25
)
does not converge weakly in a natural space
17
17

17

For example,
in the weakly nonlinear regime, the support of the limiting
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
constructed in Theorem
1.8
(i)
is contained in the space
\mathcal{A}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\supset\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{3}{4}}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
.

\mathcal{A}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
(see (
4.3
) below)
for the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure.
See Proposition
4.4
.

We first state the construction of the reference measure.
Let
p_{t}
be the kernel of the heat semigroup
e^{t\Delta}
.
Then, define the space
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
via the norm:

\displaystyle\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}:=\sup_{0<t\leq 1}\Big(t^{\frac{3}{8}}\|p_{t}\ast u\|_{L^{3}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}\Big).

(4.3)

Recall from
[
45
, Theorem 5.3]
18
18

18

The discussion in
[
45
]

is on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
, but a slight modification yields the corresponding result on
\mathbb{T}^{d}
.

(see also
[
76
, (2.41)]
and

2

)
that

\displaystyle\mathcal{A}=B^{-\frac{3}{4}}_{3,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}).

(4.4)

In particular, the space
\mathcal{A}
contains the support of the massive Gaussian
free field
\mu
on
\mathbb{T}^{3}
and thus we have

\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}<\infty
,
\mu

See Lemma

In the following,

.
Moreover, the notation
\mathcal{A}

which we recall now

\displaystyle\|p_{t}*u\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}\leq C_{\alpha,p,q}\,t^{-\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q})}\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\alpha}u\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}

From the Schauder estimate (
