we see that
W^{-\frac{3}{4},3}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\subset\mathcal{A}
.

Given
N\in\mathbb{N}
, we set

u_{N}=\pi_{N}u
.
Then, given
\delta>0
and
N\in\mathbb{N}
, we define the measure

\nu_{N,\delta}
by

\displaystyle d\nu_{N,\delta}(u)=Z_{N,\delta}^{-1}\exp\Big(-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)d\mu(u)

(4.6)

for
N\in\mathbb{N}
and
\delta>0
,
where
R_{N}^{\diamond}
is as in (
1.24
) and

\displaystyle Z_{N,\delta}=\int\exp\Big(-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)d\mu(u).

(4.7)

Namely,
\nu_{N,\delta}
is a tamed version of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
\rho_{N}
in (
1.25
).
We prove that the sequence
\{\nu_{N,\delta}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}

converges weakly to some limiting probability measure
\nu_{\delta}
.

Proposition 4.1
.

Let
\sigma\neq 0
and
\gamma\geq 3
.
Then, given any
\delta>0
, the sequence of measures
\{\nu_{N,\delta}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}

defined in (
4.6
)
converges weakly to a unique probability measure
\nu_{\delta}
,
and similarly
Z_{N,\delta}
converges to
Z_{\delta}
.
Moreover,
\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}
is finite
\nu_{\delta}
-almost surely, and we have

d\nu_{\delta}(u)=\frac{\exp(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20})}{\int\exp(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20})d\nu_{\delta^{\prime}}(u)}d\nu_{\delta^{\prime}}(u)

(4.8)

for
\delta>\delta^{\prime}>0
.

This proposition allows us to define a
\sigma
-finite version of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure by

\displaystyle d\overline{\rho}_{\delta}=e^{\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}}d\nu_{\delta}

(4.9)

for any
\delta>0
.
At a very
formal
level,

\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}
in the exponent of (
4.9
)
and
-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}
in the exponent of (
4.6
)
cancel each other in the limit as
N\to\infty
,
and thus the right-hand side of (
4.8
)
formally looks like

Z_{\delta}^{-1}\lim_{N\to\infty}e^{-R^{\diamond}_{N}(u)}d\mu
.
While this discussion is merely formal,
it explains why we refer to the measure
\overline{\rho}_{\delta}

as
a
\sigma
-finite version of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure.
The identity (
4.8
)
shows how
\nu_{\delta}
’s for different values of
\delta>0
are related.
When
\delta=0
, the expression
Z_{\delta}\overline{\rho}_{\delta}

would formally correspond
to a limit of
e^{-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)}d\mu
, but
in order to achieve the weak convergence claimed in Proposition
4.1

and construct a
\sigma
-finite version of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure,
we need to start with a tamed version (i.e.
\delta>0
) of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure.
For the sake of concreteness, we chose a taming via the
\mathcal{A}
-norm
but it is possible to consider a different taming (say, based on some other norm)
and obtain the same result.

The next proposition shows that the
\sigma
-finite version
\overline{\rho}_{\delta}

of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure defined in (
4.9
) is not normalizable
in the strongly nonlinear regime.

Proposition 4.2
.

Let
\sigma\gg 1
and
\gamma\geq 3
.
Given
\delta>0
, let
\nu_{\delta}
be the measure constructed in Proposition
4.1

and let
\overline{\rho}_{\delta}
be as in (
4.9
).
Then, we have

\displaystyle\int 1\,d\overline{\rho}_{\delta}=\int\exp\Big(\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta}=\infty.

(4.10)

Remark 4.3
.

(i)
A slight modification
of the computation in Subsection
3.4

combined with the analysis in Subsection
4.2
presented below
(Step 1 of the proof of Proposition
4.1
)
shows that
the tamed version
\nu_{\delta}

of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure, constructed in Proposition
4.1
,
and the massive Gaussian free field
\mu

are mutually singular, just like the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
in the weakly nonlinear regime, constructed in Section
3
.
As a consequence,
the
\sigma
-finite version
\overline{\rho}_{\delta}

of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure defined in (
4.9
)
and the massive Gaussian free field
\mu

are mutually singular.

(ii)
In Appendix
A
,
we show that the limiting
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure is absolutely continuous
with respect to the shifted measure

\Law(Y(1)+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}(1)+\mathcal{W}(1))

in the weakly nonlinear regime.
A slight modification of the argument
in Appendix
A

also shows that the tamed version
\nu_{\delta}

of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
constructed in Proposition
4.1

and the
\sigma
-finite version
\overline{\rho}_{\delta}

of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure in (
4.9
)
are also absolutely continuous
with respect to the same shifted measure,
even in the strongly nonlinear regime.
See Remark
A.3
.
This shows that
the measure
\overline{\rho}_{\delta}

in (
4.9
) is a quite natural candidate
to consider
as a
\sigma
-finite version
of the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure.

As a corollary to (the proofs of)
Propositions
4.1
and
4.2
,
we show the following non-convergence result
for the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
\rho_{N}
in (
1.25
).

Proposition 4.4
.

Let
\sigma\gg 1
,
\gamma\geq 3
,
and
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
be as in (
4.3
).
Then,
the sequence
\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}

of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures defined in (
1.25
)
does not converge weakly to any limit
as probability measures on
\mathcal{A}
.
The same claim holds for any subsequence

\{\rho_{N_{k}}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
.

In Subsection
4.2
,
we present the proof of Proposition
4.1
.
In Subsection
4.3
,
we then prove the non-normalizability (Proposition
4.2
).
Finally, we present the proof of Proposition
4.4

in Subsection
4.4
.

4.2.
Construction of the reference measure

In this subsection, we present the proof of Proposition
4.1

on the construction of the reference measure
\nu_{\delta}
.
We first establish several preliminary lemmas.

Lemma 4.5
.

Let the
\mathcal{A}
-norm be as in (
4.3
).
Then, we have

\displaystyle\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}\lesssim\|u\|_{H^{-\frac{1}{4}}}.

Proof.

This is immediate from the Schauder estimate (
4.5
).
∎

Lemma 4.6
.

We have
W^{-\frac{3}{4},3}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\subset\mathcal{A}
and thus the quantity
\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}

is finite
\mu
-almost surely.
Moreover, given any
1\leq p<\infty
, we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\Big[\|\pi_{N}u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{p}\Big]\leq C_{p}<\infty,

(4.11)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}
with the understanding that
\pi_{\infty}=\Id
.

Proof.

As we already mentioned, the first claim follows
from the Schauder estimate (
4.5
)
(or from (
4.4
)).
As for the bound (
4.11
),
from the Schauder estimate (
4.5
),
Minkowski’s integral inequality, and the Wiener chaos estimate (Lemma
2.5
) with (
1.18
), we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\Big[\|\pi_{N}u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{p}\Big]

\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\Big[\|u\|_{W^{-\frac{3}{4},3}}^{p}\Big]\lesssim\Big\|\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{3}{4}}u(x)\|_{L^{p}(\mu)}\Big\|_{L^{3}_{x}}^{p}

\displaystyle\leq p^{\frac{p}{2}}\Big\|\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{3}{4}}u(x)\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}\Big\|_{L^{3}_{x}}^{p}

\displaystyle\leq p^{\frac{p}{2}}\bigg(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{1}{\langle n\rangle^{\frac{7}{2}}}\bigg)^{p}<\infty.

This proves (
4.11
).
∎

We now present the proof of Proposition
4.1
.

Proof of Proposition
4.1
.

\bullet

Step 1:

In this first part, we prove that
Z_{N,\delta}
in (
4.7
) is uniformly bounded in
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
As for the tightness of
\{\nu_{N,\delta}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
and the uniqueness of
\nu_{\delta}

claimed in the statement,
we can repeat arguments analogous to those in Subsections
3.2
and
3.3

and thus we omit details.

From (
4.7
) and
the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
) with
the change of variables (
3.12
),
we have

\begin{split}-\log Z_{N,\delta}&=\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\delta\|Y_{N}+\Theta_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Theta_{N}^{2}dx-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Theta_{N}^{3}dx\\
&\hphantom{XXXXX}+A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{\gamma}\\
&\hphantom{XXXXX}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg],\end{split}

(4.12)

where

\Theta_{N}=\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}

with
\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}=\pi_{N}\mathfrak{Z}_{N}
as in (
3.19
).
Our goal is to establish a uniform lower bound on the right-hand side
of (
4.12
).
Unlike Subsection
3.2
,
we do not assume smallness on
|\sigma|
.
In this case, a rescue comes from the extra positive term

\delta\|Y_{N}+\Theta_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}
as compared to (
3.17
).

Given any
0<c_{0}<1
,
it follows from Young’s inequality (
3.40
) with
\gamma\geq 3
that

\displaystyle\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{\gamma}\geq c_{0}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{3}-C.

(4.13)

Then, taking an expectation and applying
Lemmas
3.5
and
3.6

with
Lemma
3.2
and (
3.25
), we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Bigg[A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{\gamma}\Bigg]\geq C_{0}\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}\Big]-C_{1}\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\Big]-C

(4.14)

for some
C_{0}>0
and
0<C_{1}\leq\frac{1}{4}
.
Hence,
it follows from (
4.12
), (
4.14
),
and Lemma
3.5
together with
Lemma
3.2
and (
3.25
) that
there exists
C_{2}>0
such that

\displaystyle\begin{split}-\log Z_{N,\delta}&\geq\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\delta\|Y_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N})^{3}dx\\
&\hphantom{XXXXXX}+C_{2}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+C_{2}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\bigg]-C.\end{split}

(4.15)

By Young’s inequality, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}dx\bigg|+\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}^{2}dx\bigg|&\leq\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{2}\\
&\leq\frac{C_{2}}{2|\sigma|}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{c}+C_{\sigma}.\end{split}

(4.16)

Hence, from (
4.15
) and (
4.16
)
with (
3.40
) (with
\gamma=20
) and Lemma
4.6
,
we obtain

\begin{split}-\log Z_{N,\delta}\geq\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}_{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[&\,\frac{\delta}{2}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-\frac{|\sigma|}{3}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{3}}^{3}\\
&+\frac{C_{2}}{2}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+C_{2}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\bigg]-C.\end{split}

(4.17)

Now, we need to estimate the
L^{3}
-norm of
\Upsilon_{N}
.
From (
4.3
), Sobolev’s inequality,
and the mean value theorem:
|1-e^{-t|n|^{2}}|\lesssim(t|n|^{2})^{\theta}
for any
0\leq\theta\leq 1
,
we have

\displaystyle\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{3}}^{3}

\displaystyle\lesssim t^{-\frac{9}{8}}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{3}+\|\Upsilon_{N}-p_{t}\ast\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{\frac{1}{2}}}^{3}

\displaystyle\lesssim t^{-\frac{9}{8}}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{3}+t^{\frac{3}{4}}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{3}

for
0<t\leq 1
.
By choosing
t^{\frac{3}{4}}\sim\big(1+\frac{|\sigma|}{C_{2}}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}\big)^{-1}

and applying Young’s inequality, we obtain

\displaystyle|\sigma|\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{3}}^{3}

\displaystyle\leq C_{C_{2},|\sigma|}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{\frac{3}{2}}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{3}+\frac{C_{2}}{4}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+1

(4.18)

\displaystyle\leq C_{C_{2},|\sigma|,\delta}+\frac{\delta}{4}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}+\frac{C_{2}}{2}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}.

Therefore,
from (
4.17
) and (
4.18
),
we conclude that

Z_{N,\delta}\leq C_{\delta}<\infty,

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
.

\bullet

Step 2:

Next, we show that
\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}
is finite
\nu_{\delta}
-almost surely.
Let
\eta
be a smooth function with compact support with

\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|\eta(\xi)|^{2}d\xi=1

and set

\widehat{\rho}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\eta(\xi-\xi_{1})\overline{\eta(-\xi_{1})}d\xi_{1}.

Given
\varepsilon>0
,
define
\rho_{\varepsilon}
by

\displaystyle\rho_{\varepsilon}(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\widehat{\rho}(\varepsilon n)e^{in\cdot x}.

(4.19)

Since the support of
\widehat{\rho}
is compact,
the sum on the right-hand side is over finitely many frequencies.
Thus, given any
\varepsilon>0
, there exists
N_{0}(\varepsilon)\in\mathbb{N}
such that

\displaystyle\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u=\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}

(4.20)

for any
N\geq N_{0}(\varepsilon)
.
From the Poisson summation formula, we have

\rho_{\varepsilon}(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\varepsilon^{-3}\big|\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}^{-1}(\eta)(\varepsilon^{-1}x+2\pi n)\big|^{2}\geq 0,

where
\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}^{-1}
denotes the inverse Fourier transform on
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.
Noting that

\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3})}=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\rho_{\varepsilon}(x)dx=\widehat{\rho}(0)=\|\eta\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}^{2}=1,

we have, from Young’s inequality, that

\displaystyle\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u\|_{\mathcal{A}}\leq\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}.

(4.21)

Moreover,
\{\rho_{\varepsilon}\}
defined above
is an approximation to the identity on
\mathbb{T}^{3}

and thus for any distribution
u
on
\mathbb{T}^{3}
,

\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u\to u
in the
\mathcal{A}
-norm, as
\varepsilon\to 0
.

Let
\delta>\delta^{\prime}>0
.
By Fatou’s lemma, the weak convergence of
\{\nu_{N,\delta}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}

from Step 1
with (
4.20
), (
4.21
),
and the definition (
4.6
) of
\nu_{N,\delta}
,
we have

\displaystyle\int\exp\Big((\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta}

\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int\exp\Big((\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta}

\displaystyle=\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\exp\Big((\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{N,\delta}

\displaystyle\leq\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\exp\Big((\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{N,\delta}

\displaystyle=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{Z_{N,\delta^{\prime}}}{Z_{N,\delta}}\int 1\,d\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=\frac{Z_{\delta^{\prime}}}{Z_{\delta}}.

Hence, we have

\displaystyle\int\exp\Big((\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta}<\infty

for any
\delta>\delta^{\prime}>0
.
By choosing
\delta^{\prime}=\frac{\delta}{2}
,
we obtain

\displaystyle\int\exp\Big(\frac{\delta}{2}\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta}<\infty,

which shows
that
\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}
is finite almost surely
with respect to
\nu_{\delta}
.

\bullet

Step 3:

Finally, we prove the relation (
4.8
).
We first note that it suffices to show that

\displaystyle\frac{Z_{\delta}}{Z_{\delta^{\prime}}}d\nu_{\delta}=\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta^{\prime}}

(4.22)

for any
\delta>\delta^{\prime}>0
.
In fact, once we have (
4.22
),
by integration, we obtain

\displaystyle\frac{Z_{\delta}}{Z_{\delta^{\prime}}}=\int\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta^{\prime}}

(4.23)

and thus (
4.8
) follows from (
4.22
) and (
4.23
).

Let
F:\mathcal{C}^{-100}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\to\mathbb{R}
be a bounded Lipschitz function with
F\geq 0
.
The dominated convergence theorem, the weak convergence of
\{\nu_{N,\delta}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}

from Step 1, and (
4.6
) yield that

\displaystyle\frac{Z_{\delta}}{Z_{\delta^{\prime}}}\int F(u)d\nu_{\delta}-\int F(u)\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta^{\prime}}

\displaystyle=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\bigg(\frac{Z_{\delta}}{Z_{\delta^{\prime}}}\int F(u)d\nu_{\delta}-\int F(u)\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta^{\prime}}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\lim_{N\to\infty}\bigg(\frac{Z_{N,\delta}}{Z_{N,\delta^{\prime}}}\int F(u)d\nu_{N,\delta}-\int F(u)\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\lim_{N\to\infty}\int F(u)\Big[\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)-\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)\Big]d\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}.

Therefore, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg|\frac{Z_{\delta}}{Z_{\delta^{\prime}}}&\int F(u)d\nu_{\delta}-\int F(u)\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta^{\prime}}\bigg|\\
&\lesssim\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\limsup_{N\to\infty}\int\Big|\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)\\
&\hphantom{XXXXXXXXXX}-\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)\Big|\,d\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}(u)\\
&\lesssim\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\limsup_{N\to\infty}\int\Big|\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|\pi_{N}u^{N}(\omega)\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)\\
&\hphantom{XXXXXXXXXX}-\exp\Big(-(\delta-\delta^{\prime})\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast\pi_{N}u^{N}(\omega)\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)\Big|\,d\mathbb{P}(\omega),\end{split}

(4.24)

where
u^{N}
is a random variable with
\Law(u^{N})=\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}
.
Noting that the integrand is uniformly bounded by
2
,
it follows from the bounded convergence theorem that
the right-hand side of (
4.24
) tends to 0
once we show that

\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast\pi_{N}u^{N}(\omega)-\pi_{N}u^{N}(\omega)\|_{\mathcal{A}}
tends to 0
in measure (with respect to
\mathbb{P}
).
Namely, it suffices to show

\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}

\displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\big(\{\omega\in\Omega:\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast\pi_{N}u^{N}(\omega)-\pi_{N}u^{N}(\omega)\|_{\mathcal{A}}>\alpha\}\big)

\displaystyle=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\lim_{N\to\infty}\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}\big(\big\{\|u_{N}-\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}>\alpha\}\big)=0

for any
\alpha>0
.

From (
4.3
) and (
4.5
), we have

\displaystyle\|u_{N}-\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}\lesssim\|u_{N}-\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{3}{4},3}}\lesssim\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{8}}\|u_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}.

(4.25)

Hence, from Chebyshev’s inequality and (
4.25
),
it suffices to prove

\int\|u_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}d\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}\lesssim\int\exp\big(\|u_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}\big)d\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}\leq C_{\delta^{\prime}}<\infty,

(4.26)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
We use the variational formulation as in (
4.12
), and write

\displaystyle-

\displaystyle\log\bigg(\int\exp\big(\|u_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}\big)d\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\delta^{\prime}\|Y_{N}+\Theta_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-\|Y_{N}+\Theta_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}-\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Theta_{N}^{2}dx

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXXXX}-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Theta_{N}^{3}dx+A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{\gamma}

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXXXX}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]

\displaystyle\phantom{X}+\log Z_{N,\delta^{\prime}},

where

\Theta_{N}=\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}
.
From
Lemma
3.2

and (
3.25
),
we have, for any finite
p\geq 1
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\|Y_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}^{p}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}^{p}\Big]<\infty,

(4.27)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
. See also the proof of Lemma
4.6
.
Then,
arguing as in (
4.17
) and (
4.18
) with Young’s inequality,
Sobolev’s inequality, and (
4.27
), we obtain

\displaystyle-

\displaystyle\log\bigg(\int\exp\big(\|u_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}\big)d\nu_{N,\delta^{\prime}}\bigg)

\displaystyle\geq\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}+C_{0}\big(\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{6}+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\big)+\frac{\delta^{\prime}}{4}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\bigg]-C_{C_{0},\delta^{\prime}}

\displaystyle\gtrsim-1.

This proves
(
4.26
)
and hence
concludes the proof of Proposition
4.1
.
∎

4.3.
Non-normalizability
of the
\sigma
-finite measure

In this subsection, we present the proof of Proposition

of the

-measure defined in (

Given

, let

be as in (

).
Then, by (

), the weak convergence of

\displaystyle\int

\displaystyle\exp\Big(\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta}\geq\int\exp\Big(\delta\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{\delta}

\displaystyle\geq\limsup_{L\to\infty}\int\exp\Big(\delta\min\big(\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},L\big)\Big)d\nu_{\delta}

\displaystyle=\limsup_{L\to\infty}\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\exp\Big(\delta\min\big(\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},L\big)\Big)d\nu_{N,\delta}

\displaystyle=\limsup_{L\to\infty}\lim_{N\to\infty}Z_{N,\delta}^{-1}\int\exp\Big(\delta\min\big(\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},L\big)-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)d\mu(u).

Hence, (

) is reduced to showing that

\displaystyle\limsup_{L\to\infty}\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\Big[\exp\Big(\delta\min\big(\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},L\big)-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)\Big]=\infty.

(4.28)

Let
Y=Y(1)
be as in (
3.2
).
By the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
)
with the change of variables (

),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}-&\log\mathbb{E}\Big[\exp\Big(\delta\min\big(\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},L\big)-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)\Big]\\
&=\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-\delta\min\big(\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast(Y_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N})\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},L\big)+\delta\|Y_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\\
&\hphantom{XXXXXXX}+\widehat{R}_{N}^{\diamond}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg],\end{split}

(4.29)

where

is as in (

With

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg|&\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\Theta_{N}^{2}dx\bigg|=\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}(\Upsilon_{N}^{2}+2\sigma\Upsilon_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}+\sigma^{2}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}^{2})dx\bigg|\\
&\leq C_{\sigma}\Big(1+\|Y_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{c}+\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{c}\Big)+\frac{1}{100|\sigma|}\Big(\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{3}+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\Big).\end{split}

(4.30)

By Young’s inequality,
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Theta_{N}^{3}dx-\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}^{3}dx\bigg|&=\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(3\sigma\Upsilon_{N}^{2}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}+3\sigma^{2}\Upsilon_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}^{2}+\sigma^{3}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}^{3}\Big)dx\bigg|\\
&\leq C_{\sigma}\|\mathfrak{Z}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1-\varepsilon}}^{3}+\frac{1}{100|\sigma|}\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{3}.\end{split}

(4.31)

Then, applying (
4.30
) and (
4.31
)
with
Lemma
3.2
and
(

) to (

),
we obtain

\displaystyle\begin{split}-&\log\mathbb{E}\Big[\exp\Big(\delta\min\big(\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},L\big)-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)\Big]\\
&\leq\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-\delta\min\big(\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast(Y_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N})\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},L\big)+\delta\|Y_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\\
&\hphantom{XXXXX}-\frac{\sigma}{3}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}^{3}dx+\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{L^{2}}^{3}+A\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Big(:\!Y_{N}^{2}\!:+2Y_{N}\Theta_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}\Big)dx\bigg|^{\gamma}\\
&\hphantom{XXXXX}+\frac{3}{4}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]+C_{\sigma},\end{split}

(4.32)

where
\Theta_{N}=\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}
.

In the following, we show that
the right-hand side of (
4.32
) tends to
-\infty

as
N,L\to\infty
, provided that
|\sigma|>0
is sufficiently large.
By following the strategy introduced in our previous works

[
54
,
61
]
,
we construct a drift
\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}
, achieving this goal.
The main idea is to construct a drift
\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}

such that
\Upsilon^{N}

looks like “
-Y(1)+

a perturbation” (see (
4.41
)), where the perturbation term is bounded in
L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{3})

but has a large cubic integral (see (
4.36
) below).
While we do not make use of solitons in this paper,
one should think of this perturbation as something like a soliton
or a finite blowup solution (at a fixed time)
with a highly concentrated profile.

Remark 4.7
.

While our construction of the drift
follows that in
[
54
]
,
we need to proceed more carefully in our current problem
in handling the first two terms under the expectation in (
4.32
).
If we simply apply
(
3.40
) (with
\gamma=20
)
to separate
\Upsilon_{N}
from
Y_{N}
and
\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}
,
we end up with an expression like

-\delta\min\Big(\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},L\Big)+2\delta\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}

such that the coefficients of

\|\rho_{\varepsilon}\ast\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}
and

\|\Upsilon_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}
no longer agree, which causes a serious trouble.
We instead need to keep the same coefficient
for the first two terms under the expectation in (
4.32
)
and make use of the difference structure.
Compare this with the analysis in
[
54
,
61
]
,
where no such cancellation was needed.

Fix a parameter
M\gg 1
.
Let
f:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}
be a real-valued Schwartz function
such that
the Fourier transform
\widehat{f}
is a smooth even non-negative function
supported
\big\{\frac{1}{2}<|\xi|\leq 1\}
such that
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|\widehat{f}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi=1
.
Define a function
f_{M}
on
\mathbb{T}^{3}
by

\displaystyle f_{M}(x)

\displaystyle:=M^{-\frac{3}{2}}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\widehat{f}\Big(\frac{n}{M}\Big)e_{n},

(4.33)

where
\widehat{f}
denotes the Fourier transform on
\mathbb{R}^{3}
defined by

\displaystyle\widehat{f}(\xi)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}f(x)e^{-in\cdot x}dx.

Then, a direct calculation shows the following lemma.

Lemma 4.8
.

For any
M\in\mathbb{N}
and
\alpha>0
, we have

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}f_{M}^{2}dx

\displaystyle=1+O(M^{-\alpha}),

(4.34)

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-1}f_{M})^{2}dx

\displaystyle\lesssim M^{-2},

(4.35)

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}|f_{M}|^{3}dx\sim\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}f_{M}^{3}dx

\displaystyle\sim M^{\frac{3}{2}}.

(4.36)

Proof.

As for (
4.34
) and (
4.35
),
see the proof of Lemma 5.13 in
[
54
]
.
From (
4.33
) and the fact that
\widehat{f}
is supported on
\{\frac{1}{2}<|\xi|\leq 1\}
,
we have

\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}f_{M}^{3}dx=M^{-\frac{9}{2}}\sum_{n_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\widehat{f}\Big(\frac{n_{1}}{M}\Big)\widehat{f}\Big(\frac{n_{2}}{M}\Big)\widehat{f}\Big(-\frac{n_{1}+n_{2}}{M}\Big)\sim M^{\frac{3}{2}}.

(4.37)

The bound
\|f_{M}\|_{L^{3}}^{3}\gtrsim M^{\frac{3}{2}}

follows from (
4.37
),
while
\|f_{M}\|_{L^{3}}^{3}\lesssim M^{\frac{3}{2}}

follows from Hausdorff-Young’s inequality.
This proves (
4.36
).
∎

We define
Z_{M}
and
\alpha_{M}
by

\displaystyle Z_{M}:=\sum_{|n|\leq M}\widehat{Y\big(\tfrac{1}{2})}(n)e_{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\alpha_{M}:=\mathbb{E}\big[Z_{M}^{2}(x)\big].

(4.38)

Note that
\alpha_{M}
is independent of
x\in\mathbb{T}^{3}

thanks to
the spatial translation invariance of
Z_{M}
.
Then, we have the following lemma.
See Lemma 5.14 in
[
54
]
for the proof.

Lemma 4.9
.

Let
M\gg 1
and
1\leq p<\infty
.
Then, we have

\displaystyle\alpha_{M}\sim M,

(4.39)

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}|Z_{M}|^{p}dx\bigg]\leq C(p)M^{\frac{p}{2}},

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Z_{M}^{2}dx-\alpha_{M}\Big)^{2}\bigg]+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}Z_{M}dx-\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Z_{M}^{2}dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]\lesssim 1,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}f_{M}dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Z_{M}f_{M}dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]\lesssim M^{-2}

for any

.

We now present the proof of Proposition

),
we have

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}

\displaystyle\bigg[\Big|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!(Y_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N})^{2}\!:dx\Big|^{\gamma}\bigg]

\displaystyle\leq C(\gamma)\Bigg\{\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:\!(Y_{N}+\Upsilon_{N}+\sigma\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N})^{2}\!:dx\Big|^{2}\bigg]\Bigg\}^{\frac{\gamma}{2}}

\displaystyle=C(\gamma)\Bigg\{\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:{Y_{N}^{2}}:dx+\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(\Upsilon_{N}^{2}+2Y_{N}\Upsilon_{N})dx+\sigma^{2}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}^{2}dx

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXXXX}+2\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}dx+2\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}dx\Big|^{2}\bigg]\Bigg\}^{\frac{\gamma}{2}}

\displaystyle\leq C(\gamma)\Bigg\{\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}:{Y_{N}^{2}}:dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]+\sigma^{4}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}^{2}dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXX}+\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\Upsilon_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]+\sigma^{2}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}\widetilde{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXX}+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(-\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}Z_{M}dx+\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Z_{M}^{2}dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXX}+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Z_{M}^{2}dx-\alpha_{M}\Big)^{2}\bigg]+\alpha_{M}^{2}\bigg(-1+\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}f_{M}^{2}dx\bigg)^{2}

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXX}+\alpha_{M}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Y_{N}f_{M}dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]+\alpha_{M}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big(\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}Z_{M}f_{M}dx\Big)^{2}\bigg]\Bigg\}^{\frac{\gamma}{2}}

\displaystyle\leq C(\sigma,\gamma),

which yields the bound (
4.51
).
∎

4.4.
Non-convergence of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures

In this subsection, we present the proof of
Proposition
4.4

on non-convergence of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\{\rho_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
.

We first define a slightly different tamed version of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
by setting

\displaystyle d\nu_{\delta}^{(N)}(u)=(Z_{\delta}^{(N)})^{-1}\exp\Big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)d\mu(u)

(4.57)

for
N\in\mathbb{N}
and
\delta>0
,
where the
\mathcal{A}
-norm and
R_{N}^{\diamond}
are as in (
4.3
) and (
1.24
),
respectively, and

\displaystyle Z_{\delta}^{(N)}=\int\exp\Big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)d\mu(u).

As compared to
\nu_{N,\delta}
in (
4.6
),
there is no frequency cutoff
\pi_{N}
in
the taming
-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}
in (
4.57
).
As a corollary to the proof of Proposition
4.1
,
we obtain the following convergence result
for
\nu_{\delta}^{(N)}
.

Lemma 4.11
.

Let
\delta>0
,
Then, as measures on
\mathcal{C}^{-100}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
,
the sequence of measures
\{\nu_{\delta}^{(N)}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
defined in (
4.57
) converges weakly to the limiting measure

\nu_{\delta}

constructed in Proposition
4.1
.

Proof.

By the definitions (
4.6
) and (
4.57
) of
\nu_{N,\delta}
and
\nu_{\delta}^{(N)}
, it suffices to prove

\displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\bigg\{

\displaystyle\int F(u)\exp\Big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)d\mu(u)

\displaystyle-\int F(u)\exp\Big(-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)d\mu(u)\bigg\}=0

for any bounded continuous function

F:\mathcal{C}^{-100}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\to\mathbb{R}
.
In the following, we prove

\displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\Big|\exp\Big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)-\exp\Big(-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)\Big|d\mu(u)=0.

(4.58)

By the uniform boundedness of the frequency projector
\pi_{N}
on
\mathcal{A}
,
we have

\displaystyle\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}\lesssim\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}},

(4.59)

uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
Then, it follows from the mean-value theorem, (
4.59
),
and the Schauder estimate (
4.5
)
that there exists
c_{0}>0
such that

\displaystyle\begin{split}\int&\Big|\exp\Big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)-\exp\Big(-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)\Big|\,d\mu(u)\\
&\lesssim\delta\int\exp\Big(-\delta\min\big(\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20},\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\big)-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)\big|\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\big|\,d\mu(u)\\
&\lesssim\delta\int\exp\Big(-\delta c_{0}\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)\|u-u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{19}d\mu(u)\\
&\lesssim\delta\int\exp\Big(-\delta c_{0}\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)N^{-\frac{1}{8}}\|u\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}^{20}d\mu(u).\end{split}

(4.60)

In the last step, we used the following bound:

\|u-u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}\lesssim\|\pi_{N}^{\perp}u\|_{W^{-\frac{3}{4},3}}\lesssim N^{-\frac{1}{8}}\|u\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}},

which follows from
(
4.3
), (
4.5
), and the fact that

\pi_{N}^{\perp}u=u-u_{N}
has the frequency support
\{|n|\gtrsim N\}
.
Therefore, by (
4.6
), Proposition
4.1
, and (
4.26
), we obtain

\displaystyle\limsup_{N\to\infty}

\displaystyle\int\Big|\exp\Big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)-\exp\Big(-\delta\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)\Big|d\mu(u)

\displaystyle\lesssim\delta\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\exp\Big(-\delta c_{0}\|u_{N}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)N^{-\frac{1}{8}}\|u\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}^{20}d\mu(u)

\displaystyle=\delta\lim_{N\to\infty}N^{-\frac{1}{8}}Z_{N,c_{0}\delta}\int\|u\|_{W^{-\frac{5}{8},3}}^{20}d\nu_{N,c_{0}\delta}

\displaystyle=0.

This proves (
4.58
).
∎

Remark 4.12
.

In the penultimate step of
(
4.60
), we used the boundedness of the cube frequency projector
\pi_{N}=\pi_{N}^{\text{cube}}

on
L^{3}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
and hence
this argument
does not work
for the ball frequency projector
\pi_{N}^{\text{ball}}

defined in (
1.41
).

We conclude this section by presenting the proof of Proposition
4.4
.

Proof of Proposition
4.4
.

Suppose by contradiction that, as probability measures on
\mathcal{A}
,

\{\rho_{N_{k}}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}

has a weak limit
\nu_{0}
.
Then, given any

\delta>0
, from Lemma
4.11

with (
4.57
) and (
1.25
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}d\nu_{\delta}&=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\exp\Big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N_{k}}^{\diamond}(u)\Big)}{\int\exp\Big(-\delta\|v\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}-R_{N_{k}}^{\diamond}(v)\Big)d\mu(v)}d\mu(u)\\
&=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\exp\big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\big)}{\int\exp\big(-\delta\|v\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\big)d\rho_{N_{k}}(v)}d\rho_{N_{k}}(u)\\
&=\frac{\exp\big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\big)}{\int\exp\big(-\delta\|v\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\big)d\nu_{0}(v)}d\nu_{0}(u),\end{split}

(4.61)

where the limits are interpreted as weak limits of measures on
\mathcal{C}^{-100}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
.
Note that, in the last step, we used the weak convergence in
\mathcal{A}
of the
truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\rho_{N_{k}}
, since
\exp(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20})
is continuous on
\mathcal{A}
, but not on
\mathcal{C}^{-100}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
.
Therefore, from (
4.61
) and (
4.9
), we obtain

\displaystyle d\nu_{0}(u)=\bigg(\int\exp\big(-\delta\|v\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\big)d\nu_{0}(v)\bigg)d\overline{\rho}_{\delta}(u).

(4.62)

By assumption,
\nu_{0}
is a probability measure on
\mathcal{A}

and thus
\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}<\infty
,
\nu_{0}
-almost surely.
By the fact that
\nu_{0}
is a probability measure, (
4.62
),
and Proposition
4.2
,
we obtain

\displaystyle 1

\displaystyle=\int 1\,d\nu_{0}

\displaystyle=\int\exp\Big(-\delta\|u\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{20}\Big)d\nu_{0}(u)\int 1\,d\overline{\rho}_{\delta}(u)

\displaystyle=\infty,

which yields a
contradiction.
Therefore,
no subsequence of the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\rho_{N}
has a weak limit
as probability measures on
\mathcal{A}
.
∎

5.
Local well-posedness

In this section,
we present the proof of Theorem
1.14
on
local well-posedness
of the (renormalized) hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
1.33

\displaystyle\partial_{t}^{2}u+\partial_{t}u+(1-\Delta)u-\sigma:\!u^{2}\!:+M(\,:\!u^{2}\!:\,)u=\sqrt{2}\xi,

(5.1)

where
M
is defined as in (
1.34
).
For the local theory, the size of
\sigma\neq 0
does not play any role
and hence we set
\sigma=1
in the remaining part of this section.
As mentioned in Section
1
,
local well-posedness of (
5.1
)
follows from a slight modification of the argument in
[
36
,
54
]
.
We, however, point out that the argument in
[
36
]

on the quadratic SNLW alone
is not sufficient due to the additional term

M(\,:\!u^{2}\!:\,)u
, coming from the taming in constructing
the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure.

5.1.
Paracontrolled approach

In this subsection, we
go over a paracontrolled approach to rewrite the equation (
5.1
)
into a system of three unknowns.
While our presentation closely follows those in
[
36
,
54
]

we present some details for readers’ convenience.
Proceeding
in the spirit of

[
18

48

36

54

we
transform the quadratic SdNLW (

In order to treat the additional term

in (
5.1

which contains an ill-defined product in
:\!u^{2}\!:\,

we follow the approach
in our previous work
[

which leads to

Compare this with
[

At the end of this subsection,
we state a local well-posedness result

The main difficulty in studying the hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
5.1
)
comes from the roughness of the space-time white noise.
This is already manifested at the level of the linear equation.
Let
\Psi
denote the stochastic convolution, satisfying

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\partial_{t}^{2}\Psi+\partial_{t}\Psi+(1-\Delta)\Psi=\sqrt{2}\xi\\

where

the Gaussian random distributions with

\Law(\phi_{0}^{\omega},\phi_{1}^{\omega})=\vec{\mu}=\mu\otimes\mu_{0}

Define the linear damped wave propagator

by

\mathcal{D}(t)=e^{-\frac{t}{2}}\frac{\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\tfrac{3}{4}-\Delta}\Big)}{\sqrt{\tfrac{3}{4}-\Delta}}

viewed as a Fourier multiplier operator.
By setting

\displaystyle[\hskip-1.70717pt[n]\hskip-1.70717pt]=\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{2}},

(5.2)

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}(t)f=e^{-\frac{t}{2}}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{\sin(t[\hskip-1.70717pt[n]\hskip-1.70717pt])}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n]\hskip-1.70717pt]}\widehat{f}(n)e_{n}.

(5.3)

Then, the stochastic convolution

can be expressed as

\Psi(t)=S(t)(\phi_{0},\phi_{1})+\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})dW(t^{\prime}),

where

\displaystyle S(t)(f,g)=\partial_{t}\mathcal{D}(t)f+\mathcal{D}(t)(f+g)

It is easy to see that

In the following, we use

to denote
a small positive constant, which can be arbitrarily small.

In the following, we adopt Hairer’s convention to denote the stochastic terms by trees;
the vertex “

\xi

while the edge denotes the Duhamel integral operator

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(F)(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})F(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}=\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\frac{t-t^{\prime}}{2}}\frac{\sin\Big((t-t^{\prime})\sqrt{\tfrac{3}{4}-\Delta}\Big)}{\sqrt{\tfrac{3}{4}-\Delta}}F(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}.

(5.6)

With a slight abuse of notation,

\displaystyle\immediate\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}:=\Psi,

(5.7)

Theorem 5.1
.

Let

\frac{1}{4}<s_{1}<\frac{1}{2}<s_{2}\leq s_{1}+\frac{1}{4}

and
s_{2}-1\leq s_{3}<0
.
Then,
there exist
\theta=\theta(s_{3})>0

and
\varepsilon=\varepsilon(s_{1},s_{2},s_{3})>0

such that
if

•

is a distribution-valued function belonging to

C([0,1];W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))\cap C^{1}([0,1];W^{-\frac{3}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
,

•

is a distribution-valued function belonging to
C([0,1];W^{-1-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
,

•

is a distribution-valued function belonging to

C([0,1];W^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))\cap C^{1}([0,1];W^{-1-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
,

•

is a distribution-valued function belonging to
C([0,1];H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
,

•

\mathbb{A}(t,t^{\prime})

is a distribution-valued function belonging to
L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{3}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(1);H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
,
where
\Delta_{2}(T)\subset[0,T]^{2}
is defined by

\displaystyle\Delta_{2}(T)=\{(t,t^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2}:0\leq t^{\prime}\leq t\leq T\},

5.2.
Strichartz estimates

Given
0\leq s\leq 1
,
we say that a pair
(q,r)
is
s
-admissible
(a pair
(\widetilde{q},\widetilde{r})
is dual
s
-admissible,
24
24

24

Here, we define
the notion of dual
s
-admissibility for the convenience of the presentation.
Note that
(\widetilde{q},\widetilde{r})
is dual
s
-admissible
if and only if
(\widetilde{q}^{\prime},\widetilde{r}^{\prime})
is
(1-s)
-admissible.

respectively)
if
1\leq\widetilde{q}<2<q\leq\infty
,

1<\widetilde{r}\leq 2\leq r<\infty
,

\displaystyle\frac{1}{q}+\frac{3}{r}=\frac{3}{2}-s=\frac{1}{\widetilde{q}}+\frac{3}{\widetilde{r}}-2,\qquad\frac{1}{q}+\frac{1}{r}\leq\frac{1}{2},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{1}{\widetilde{q}}+\frac{1}{\widetilde{r}}\geq\frac{3}{2}.

We say that
u
is a solution to the following nonhomogeneous linear damped wave equation:

\displaystyle\begin{cases}(\partial_{t}^{2}+\partial_{t}+1-\Delta)u=F\\
(u,\partial_{t}u)|_{t=0}=(u_{0},u_{1})\end{cases}

(5.35)

on a time interval containing
t=0
,
if
u
satisfies the following Duhamel formulation:

u=S(t)(u_{0},u_{1})+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})F(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime},

where
S(t)
and
\mathcal{D}(t)
are as in (
5.5
) and (
5.3
), respectively.
We now recall the Strichartz estimates
for solutions to the nonhomogeneous linear damped wave equation (
5.35
).

Lemma 5.3
.

Given
0\leq s\leq 1
,
let
(q,r)
and
(\widetilde{q},\widetilde{r})

be
s
-admissible and dual
s
-admissible pairs, respectively.
Then, a solution
u
to the nonhomogeneous linear damped wave equation (
5.35
)
satisfies

\displaystyle\|(u,\partial_{t}u)\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}\mathcal{H}^{s}_{x}}+\|u\|_{L^{q}_{T}L^{r}_{x}}\lesssim\|(u_{0},u_{1})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s}}+\|F\|_{L^{\widetilde{q}}_{T}L^{\widetilde{r}}_{x}}

(5.36)

for all
0<T\leq 1
.
The following estimate also holds:

\displaystyle\|(u,\partial_{t}u)\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}\mathcal{H}^{s}_{x}}+\|u\|_{L^{q}_{T}L^{r}_{x}}\lesssim\|(u_{0},u_{1})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s}}+\|F\|_{L^{1}_{T}H^{s-1}_{x}}

(5.37)

for all
0<T\leq 1
.
The same estimates also hold for any finite
T>1
but
with the implicit constants depending on
T
.

The Strichartz estimates on
\mathbb{R}^{d}
are well known; see
[
29
,
46
,
41
]

in the context of the undamped wave equation
(with the linear part
\partial_{t}^{2}-\Delta
).
For the undamped Klein-Gordon equation (with the linear part

\partial_{t}^{2}+1-\Delta
),
see
[
42
]
.
Thanks to the finite speed of propagation,
these estimates on
\mathbb{T}^{3}
follow from the corresponding
estimates on
\mathbb{R}^{3}
.

As for the current damped case,
by setting
v(t)=e^{\frac{t}{2}}u(t)
,
the damped wave equation (
5.35
) becomes

\displaystyle\begin{cases}(\partial_{t}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}-\Delta)v=e^{\frac{t}{2}}F\\
(v,\partial_{t}v)|_{t=0}=(u_{0},u_{1}),\end{cases}

to which the Strichartz estimates for the Klein-Gordon equation apply.
By undoing the transformation,
we then obtain the Strichartz estimates
for the damped equation (
5.35
)
on finite time intervals
[0,T]
,
where the implicit constants depend on
T
.

In proving Theorem
5.1
, we use the fact that

\big(8,\frac{8}{3}\big)

and
(4,4)
are
\frac{1}{4}
-admissible
and

\frac{1}{2}
-admissible, respectively.
We also use
a dual
\frac{1}{2}
-admissible pair
\big(\frac{4}{3},\frac{4}{3}\big)
.

5.3.
Stochastic terms and paracontrolled operators

In this subsection, we collect regularity properties of stochastic terms and
the paracontrolled operators. See
[
36
,
54
]

for the proofs.
Note that the stochastic objects are constructed
from the stochastic convolution
\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}=\Psi
in (
5.4
).
In particular, in the following, probabilities of various events
are measured with respect to the Gaussian initial data
and the space-time white noise.
25
25

25

With the notation in Section
6

(see (
6.4
)),
this is equivalent to saying that we measure various events with respect to
\vec{\mu}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
.

First,
we state the regularity properties of
and
.
See Lemma 3.1 in
[
36
]
and Lemma 4.1 in
[
54
]
.

Lemma 5.4
.

Let
T>0
.

(i)

For any
\varepsilon>0
,

\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}
in (

in
C([0,T];W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))\cap C^{1}([0,T];W^{-\frac{3}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))

almost surely.
In particular, we have

\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}\in C([0,T];W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))\cap C^{1}([0,T];W^{-\frac{3}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))

almost surely.
Moreover, we have
the following tail estimate:

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big(\|\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}\|_{C_{T}W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}\cap\,C^{1}_{T}W^{-\frac{3}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}>\lambda\Big)\leq C(1+T)\exp\big(-c\lambda^{2}\big)

(5.38)

for any
T>0

,
uniformly in

with the understanding that

(ii)

For any
\varepsilon>0
,

\makebox[6.09036pt][c]{\hbox to6.09036pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.23257pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}

in

In particular, we have

\makebox[6.09036pt][c]{\hbox to6.09036pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.23257pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}\in C([0,T];W^{-1-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))

almost surely.
Moreover, we have
the following tail estimate:

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big(\|\makebox[6.09036pt][c]{\hbox to6.09036pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.23257pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}\|_{C_{T}W^{-1-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}>\lambda\Big)\leq C(1+T)\exp\big(-c\lambda\big)

Lemma 5.6
.

Let
T>0
.
Then,

\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}
converges to

in

almost surely
for any
\varepsilon>0
.
In particular, we have

\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}\in C([0,T];W^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))\cap C^{1}([0,T];W^{-1-\varepsilon,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))

.

the following tail estimate:

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big(\|\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}\|_{C_{T}W^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}\cap\,C^{1}_{T}W^{-1-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}>\lambda\Big)\leq C(1+T)\exp\big(-c\lambda\big)

.

,
uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
.

Finally, we state the regularity property of

\mathbb{A}
defined in (
5.26
).
See Lemma 7.2 in
[
54
]
.
Given
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
we define the truncated version
\mathbb{A}_{N}
:

\displaystyle\mathbb{A}_{N}(x,t,t^{\prime})=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}e_{n}(x)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n=n_{1}+n_{2}\\
|n_{1}|\sim|n_{2}|\end{subarray}}e^{-\frac{t-t^{\prime}}{2}}\frac{\sin((t-t^{\prime})[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{1}]\hskip-1.70717pt])}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[n_{1}]\hskip-1.70717pt]}\widehat{\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}}_{N}(n_{1},t^{\prime})\widehat{\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}}_{N}(n_{2},t)

(5.46)

by replacing
by
\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}
in (
5.26
).

Lemma 5.10
.

Fix finite
q\geq 2
.
Then,
given any
T,\varepsilon>0
and finite
p\geq 1
,

\{\mathbb{A}_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
is a Cauchy sequence in

L^{p}(\Omega;L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T);H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})))
,
converging to some limit
\mathbb{A}

(
formally defined by (
5.26
)
)

in
L^{p}(\Omega;L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T);H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})))
,
where
\Delta_{2}(T)
is as in (
5.30
).
Moreover,
\mathbb{A}_{N}
converges almost surely to the same limit in
L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T);H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
.
Furthermore,
we have
the following uniform tail estimate
:

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big(\|\mathbb{A}_{N}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t^{\prime}}L^{q}_{t}(\Delta_{2}(T);H^{-\varepsilon}_{x})}>\lambda\Big)\leq C(1+T)\exp(-\lambda)

for any
\lambda\gg 1
, and
N\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}
,
where
\mathbb{A}_{\infty}=\mathbb{A}
.

5.4.

\displaystyle\hphantom{X}+\int_{0}^{T}|M(Q_{X,Y}+2\mathfrak{R}+\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}^{2}+2\makebox[9.07776pt][c]{\hbox to9.07776pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}+\makebox[6.09036pt][c]{\hbox to6.09036pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.23257pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}})(t^{\prime})|\cdot\|\mathbb{A}(t,t^{\prime})\|_{L^{3}_{t}([t^{\prime},T];H^{s_{3}}_{x})}dt^{\prime}

(5.56)

\displaystyle\lesssim T^{\frac{1}{3}}K^{2}\Big(\|X\|_{L_{T}^{\infty}H_{x}^{s_{1}}}+\|Y\|_{L_{T}^{\infty}H_{x}^{s_{2}}}+\|\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}W_{x}^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}}\Big)

\displaystyle\hphantom{X}+T^{\frac{1}{3}}K\|Q_{X,Y}+2\mathfrak{R}+\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}^{2}+2\makebox[9.07776pt][c]{\hbox to9.07776pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}+\makebox[6.09036pt][c]{\hbox to6.09036pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.23257pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}\|_{L_{T}^{3}H_{x}^{-100}}^{2}

\displaystyle\lesssim T^{\frac{1}{3}}K\Big(\|(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}^{4}+K^{4}\Big)

provided that

s_{1}>0
with sufficiently small
\varepsilon=\varepsilon(s_{1})>0

(in view of Lemma
5.8
),

s_{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon
, and
-100\leq s_{3}\leq-\varepsilon
.

Note that
|x|x
is differentiable with a locally bounded derivative.
In view of (
1.34
), this allows us to estimate the difference

M(w_{1})-M(w_{2})
.
By repeating a similar computation, we also obtain the difference estimate:

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\vec{\Phi}&(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})-\vec{\Phi}(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y},\widetilde{\mathfrak{R}})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}\\
&\lesssim T^{\frac{1}{4}}\Big(\|(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}^{4}+K^{4}\Big)\|(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})-(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y},\widetilde{\mathfrak{R}})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)},\end{split}

(5.57)

where

\displaystyle\vec{\Phi}:=(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2},\Phi_{3}).

Therefore, by choosing
T=T(K)>0
sufficiently small,
we conclude from (
5.53
), (
5.55
), (
5.56
), and (
5.57
) that

\vec{\Phi}=(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2},\Phi_{3})

is a contraction on the closed ball
B_{R}\subset Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)

of radius
R\sim 1+\|(X_{0},X_{1})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s_{1}}}+\|(Y_{0},Y_{1})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s_{2}}}
centered at the origin.
A similar computation yields
Lipschitz continuous dependence of the solution
(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})

on the enhanced data set
(X_{0},X_{1},Y_{0},Y_{1},\Xi)

measured in the
\mathcal{X}^{s_{1},s_{2},\varepsilon}_{T}
-norm
by possibly making
T>0
smaller.
This concludes the proof of
Theorem
5.1
.

6.
Invariant Gibbs dynamics

In this section, we present the proof of Theorem
1.15
.
In the remaining part of this section,
we work in the weakly nonlinear regime.
Namely, we fix
\sigma\neq 0
such that
|\sigma|\leq\sigma_{0}
,
where
\sigma_{0}
is as in
Theorem
1.8
(i).
We also fix sufficiently large
A\gg 1
as in
Theorem
1.8
(i)
such that the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure

\rho
is constructed as the limit of
the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\rho_{N}

in (
1.25
).
With these parameters,
consider
the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
:

\displaystyle\vec{\rho}_{N}=\rho_{N}\otimes\mu_{0}

(6.1)

for
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
where
\mu_{0}
is the white noise measure; see (
1.15
) with
s=0
.
A standard argument
[
37
,
59
,
54
]

shows that
the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
is invariant under
the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
1.38
):

\displaystyle\begin{split}\partial_{t}^{2}&u_{N}+\partial_{t}u_{N}+(1-\Delta)u_{N}\\
&-\sigma\pi_{N}\big(:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,\big)+M(\,:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,)\pi_{N}u_{N}=\sqrt{2}\xi,\end{split}

(6.2)

where

:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,=(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}

and
\pi_{N}
and
\sigma_{N}
are as in (
1.19
) and (
1.22
), respectively.
See Lemma
6.4
below.
Moreover, as a corollary to Theorem
1.8
(i),
the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
in (
6.1
) converges weakly to the Gibbs measure

\vec{\rho}=\rho\otimes\mu_{0}
in (
1.32
).

Our main goal is to construct global-in-time
dynamics for the limiting hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
1.33
)
almost surely with respect to the Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}
,
and prove invariance of the Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}
under the limiting
hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-dynamics.
A naive approach would be
to apply Bourgain’s invariant measure
argument
[
9
,
11
]
, by exploiting the invariance
of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}

under the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-dynamics,
and to
try to construct global-in-time limiting dynamics
for
the limiting process
u=\lim_{N\to\infty}u_{N}
.
There are, however, two issues in the current situation:
(i) the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
converges to the limiting Gibbs measure

\vec{\rho}

only weakly
and (ii)
the Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}
and the base Gaussian measure

\vec{\mu}=\mu\otimes\mu_{0}
in (
1.16
) are
mutually singular
.
Moreover, our local theory relies on the paracontrolled approach,
which gives additional difficulty.
As a result, Bourgain’s invariant measure
argument
[
9
,
11
]
is not directly applicable to our problem.
In
[
14
]
, Bringmann encountered a similar problem
in the context of the defocusing Hartree NLW on
\mathbb{T}^{3}
,
where he overcame this issue by introducing a new globalization argument,
by using the fact that the (truncated) Gibbs measure
is absolutely continuous with respect to a shifted measure (as in Appendix
A
below)

[
54
,
13
]
in a uniform manner
and
establishing a (rather involved) large time stability theory,
where sets of large probabilities are characterized
via the shifted measures.

In the following, we introduce a new alternative globalization
argument.
This new argument has the advantage of being
conceptually simple and straightforward.
Our approach consists of several steps:

1.

In the first step, we
establish a uniform (in
N
) exponential integrability of the truncated enhanced data set
\Xi_{N}

(see (
6.10
) below)
with respect to the truncated measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

(Proposition
6.5
).
Here,

\mathbb{P}_{2}
is the measure for the stochastic forcing
defined in (
6.4
) below.
By combining the variational approach
with space-time estimates,
we prove this uniform exponential integrability

without
any reference to (the truncated version of) the shifted measure

\Law(Y(1)+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}(1)+\mathcal{W}(1))
constructed in Appendix
A
.
As a corollary,
we construct the limiting enhanced data set
\Xi
associated with the Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}

(see (
6.11
) below)
by establishing convergence of the truncated enhanced data set
\Xi_{N}

almost surely with respect to the limiting measure
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
.

2.

In the second step, we establish a stability result (Proposition
6.8
).
We prove this stability result by a simple contraction argument,
where we use a norm with an exponentially decaying weight in time.
As a result, the proof follows from a small modification of
that of the local well-posedness (Theorem
5.1
).
As compared to
[
14
]
,
our stability argument is very simple (both in terms of the statements
and the proofs).

3.

In the third step,
we establish a uniform (in
N
) control
on the solution
(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})

to the truncated system (see (
6.58
) below)
with respect to the truncated measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

(Proposition
6.9
).
The proof is based on
the invariance of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}

and a discrete Gronwall argument.

4.

In the fourth step,
we study the pushforward measures

(\Xi_{N})_{\#}(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})

and

(\Xi)_{\#}(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})
.
In particular,
by using ideas from theory of optimal transport (the Kantorovich duality)
and the Boué-Dupuis variational formula,
we prove that the pushforward measure

(\Xi_{N})_{\#}(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})

converges to

(\Xi)_{\#}(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})

in the Wasserstein-1 distance, as
N\to\infty
;
see Proposition
6.10
below.

Once we establish Steps 1 - 4, the proof of Theorem
1.15

follows in a straightforward manner.
In Subsection
6.1
,
we first study the truncated dynamics (
6.2
)
and briefly go over almost sure global well-posedness of (
6.2
)
and invariance of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
(Lemma
6.4
).
We then discuss the details of Step 1 above.
In Subsection
6.2
,
we first go over the details of Steps 2, 3, and 4
and then present the proof of
Theorem
1.15
.

Notations:

By assumption, the Gaussian field
\vec{\mu}=\mu\otimes\mu_{0}
in (
1.16
)
and hence the (truncated) Gibbs measure
are independent of (the distribution of) the space-time white noise
\xi
in (
1.33
)
and (
6.2
).
Hence, we can write the probability space
\Omega

as

\displaystyle\Omega=\Omega_{1}\times\Omega_{2}

(6.3)

such that the random Fourier series in (
1.18
) depend only on
\omega_{1}\in\Omega_{1}
,
while the cylindrical Wiener process
W
in (
3.1
)
depends only on
\omega_{2}\in\Omega_{2}
.
In view of (
6.3
),
we also write the underlying probability measure
\mathbb{P}
on
\Omega

as

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}_{1}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2},

(6.4)

where
\mathbb{P}_{j}
is the marginal probability measure on
\Omega_{j}
,
j=1,2
.

With the decomposition (
6.3
) in mind,
we set

\displaystyle\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=S(t)\vec{u}_{0}+\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})dW(t^{\prime},\omega_{2})

(6.5)

for
\vec{u}_{0}=(u_{0},u_{1})\in\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
and
\omega_{2}\in\Omega_{2}
,
where
S(t)
and
\mathcal{D}(t)
are as in (
5.5
) and (
5.3
), respectively.
When it is clear from the context,
we may suppress the dependence on
\vec{u}_{0}
and/or
\omega_{2}
.
Given
N\in\mathbb{N}
, we set

\displaystyle\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\pi_{N}\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}),

(6.6)

where
\pi_{N}
is as in (
1.19
).
We also set

\displaystyle\begin{split}\makebox[6.09036pt][c]{\hbox to6.09036pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.23257pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})&=\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}^{2}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})-\sigma_{N},\\
\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})&=\pi_{N}\mathcal{I}(\makebox[6.09036pt][c]{\hbox to6.09036pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.23257pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})),\\
\makebox[69.4772pt][c]{\hbox to69.4772pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=17.22978pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})&=\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\mathbin{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.7}{{\hbox{\hbox to8.9pt{\vbox to8.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.45pt\lower-4.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.88 0 C 5.88 3.25 3.25 5.88 0 5.88 C -3.25 5.88 -5.88 3.25 -5.88 0 C -5.88 -3.25 -3.25 -5.88 0 -5.88 C 3.25 -5.88 5.88 -3.25 5.88 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces
}{{{{\ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{-3.06946pt}{-1.34427pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{62}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}}}{\scalebox{.7}{{\hbox{\hbox to8.9pt{\vbox to8.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.45pt\lower-4.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.88 0 C 5.88 3.25 3.25 5.88 0 5.88 C -3.25 5.88 -5.88 3.25 -5.88 0 C -5.88 -3.25 -3.25 -5.88 0 -5.88 C 3.25 -5.88 5.88 -3.25 5.88 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces

.

(iii) Note that the
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
-norm
for enhanced data sets defined in (
5.49
)
also measures
the time derivatives of
\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}
and
\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}

in appropriate space-time norms.
In view of (
6.7
) and (
5.6
),
the time derivative of
\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

is given by

\partial_{t}\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\pi_{N}\int_{0}^{t}\partial_{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})\makebox[6.09036pt][c]{\hbox to6.09036pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.23257pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(t^{\prime};\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})dt^{\prime}.

As for the stochastic convolution,
recall that, unlike the heat or Schrödinger case,
the stochastic convolution
for the damped wave equation is differentiable in time
and the time derivative of
\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

is given by

\displaystyle\partial_{t}\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\pi_{N}\partial_{t}S(t)\vec{u}_{0}+\sqrt{2}\pi_{N}\int_{0}^{t}\partial_{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})dW(t^{\prime},\omega_{2}).

(6.13)

The formula (
6.13
) easily follows
from viewing the stochastic integral in (
6.5
) (with an extra frequency cutoff
\pi_{N}
)
as a Paley-Wiener-Zygmund integral
and taking a time derivative.

6.1.
On the truncated dynamics

In this subsection, we
study the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
6.2
).
We first go over local well-posedness of the truncated equation (
6.2
)
and then almost sure global well-posedness
and invariance of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
;
see Lemmas
6.2
and
6.4
.
Then,
by combining the Boué-Dupuis variational formula
(Lemma
3.1
)
and space-time estimates,
we prove
uniform (in
N
) exponential integrability of the truncated enhanced data set

\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

with respect to
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
on
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
;
see Proposition
6.5
.
As a corollary, we prove that the truncated
enhanced data set
\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.10
)
converges to the limiting enhanced data set
\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.11
)
almost surely with respect to the limiting measure
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

(Corollary
6.7
).

Given
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
let

\vec{u}_{0}=(u_{0},u_{1})

be a pair of random distributions such that

\Law((u_{0},u_{1}))=\vec{\rho}_{N}=\rho_{N}\otimes\mu_{0}
.
Let
u_{N}
be a solution
to the truncated equation (
6.2
) with
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})|_{t=0}=\vec{u}_{0}
.
With

:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,=(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}
, we write (
6.2
) as

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}^{2}u_{N}+\partial_{t}u_{N}+(1-\Delta)u_{N}\\
&\quad-\sigma\pi_{N}\big((\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}\big)+M\big((\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}\big)\pi_{N}u_{N}=\sqrt{2}\xi\end{aligned}\\
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})|_{t=0}=\vec{u}_{0},\end{cases}

(6.14)

where

M
is as in (
1.34
).
Note that, due to the presence
of the frequency projector
\pi_{N}
,
the dynamics (
6.14
) on high frequencies
\{|n|\gtrsim N\}

and low frequencies
\{|n|\lesssim N\}

are decoupled.
The high frequency part of the dynamics (
6.14
) is given by

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}^{2}\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}+\partial_{t}\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}+(1-\Delta)\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}=\sqrt{2}\pi_{N}^{\perp}\xi\end{aligned}\\
(\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N},\partial_{t}\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N})|_{t=0}=\pi_{N}^{\perp}\vec{u}_{0}.\end{cases}

(6.15)

The solution
\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}
to (
6.15
) is given by

\displaystyle\pi_{N}^{\perp}u_{N}=\pi_{N}^{\perp}\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(\vec{u}_{0}),

(6.16)

where
\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(\vec{u}_{0})
is as in (
6.5
)
with the
\omega_{2}
-dependence suppressed.
With
v_{N}=\pi_{N}u_{N}
,
the low frequency part of the dynamics (
6.14
) is given by

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}^{2}v_{N}+\partial_{t}v_{N}+(1-\Delta)v_{N}\\
&\quad-\sigma\pi_{N}\big((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}\big)+M\big((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}\big)\pi_{N}v_{N}=\sqrt{2}\pi_{N}\xi\end{aligned}\\
(v_{N},\partial_{t}v_{N})|_{t=0}=\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0},\end{cases}

(6.17)

where we kept
\pi_{N}
in several places to emphasize that
(
6.17
) depends only on finite many
frequencies
\{n\in NQ\}
with
Q
as in (
1.21
).
By writing (
6.17
) in the Duhamel formulation,
we have

\displaystyle v_{N}(t)=\pi_{N}S(t)\vec{u}_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{N}_{N}(v_{N})(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}+\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(t;0),

(6.18)

where the truncated nonlinearity
\mathcal{N}_{N}(v_{N})
is given by

\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{N}(v_{N})=\sigma\pi_{N}\big((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}\big)-M\big((\pi_{N}v_{N})^{2}-\sigma_{N}\big)\pi_{N}v_{N}.

(6.19)

and
\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(t;0)
is as in (
6.6
) with
\vec{u}_{0}=0
:

\displaystyle\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(t;0,\omega_{2})=\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})\pi_{N}dW(t^{\prime},\omega_{2}).

For each fixed
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
we have

\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(t;0)=\pi_{N}\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(t;0)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
; see Remark
6.1
.
By viewing
\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(t;0)
in (
6.18
) as a perturbation,
it suffices to study
the following damped NLW with a deterministic perturbation:

\displaystyle v_{N}(t)=\pi_{N}S(t)(v_{0},v_{1})+\int_{0}^{t}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{N}_{N}(v_{N})(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}+F,

(6.20)

where
(v_{0},v_{1})\in\mathcal{H}^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
,
\sigma_{N}
is as in (
1.22
), and

F\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
is a given deterministic function.

A standard contraction argument
with the one degree of smoothing from the Duhamel integral operator
\mathcal{I}
in (
5.6
)
and Sobolev’s inequality yields the following local well-posedness
of (
6.20
).
Since the argument is standard, we omit details.
See, for example, the proof of Lemma 9.1 in
[
54
]
.

Lemma 6.2
.

Let
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
Given any

(v_{0},v_{1})\in\mathcal{H}^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3})
and
F\in C^{1}([0,1];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
with

\|(v_{0},v_{1})\|_{\mathcal{H}^{1}}\leq R\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|F\|_{C^{1}([0,1];H^{1})}\leq K

for some
R,K\geq 1
,
there exist
\tau=\tau(R,K,N)>0
and a unique solution
v_{N}

to (
6.20
) on
[0,\tau]
,
satisfying the bound
:

\|v_{N}\|_{\widetilde{X}^{1}(\tau)}\lesssim R+K,

where

\displaystyle\widetilde{X}^{1}(\tau)=C([0,\tau];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))\cap C^{1}([0,\tau];L^{2}(\mathbb{T}^{3})).

Moreover, the solution
v_{N}
is unique
in
\widetilde{X}^{1}(\tau)
.

Remark 6.3
.

(i) A standard contraction argument gives

\tau=\tau(R,K,N)\sim(R+K+N)^{-\theta}

for some
\theta>0
,
in particular the local existence
depends on
N\in\mathbb{N}
.

(ii)
We also point out that the uniqueness statement
for
v_{N}
in Lemma
6.2
is unconditional,
namely, the uniqueness of the solution
v_{N}
holds in the entire class

\widetilde{X}^{1}(\tau)
.
Then, from (
6.16
) and
the unconditional uniqueness of the solution
v_{N}=v_{N}(\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0})
to (
6.17
),
we obtain the
unique
representation of
u_{N}
:

u_{N}=\pi_{N}^{\perp}\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(\vec{u}_{0})+v_{N}(\pi_{N}\vec{u}_{0}).

See for example (
6.129
) below,
where we use a different representation of
u_{N}
.

Before proceeding further, let us introduce some notations.
Given the cylindrical Wiener process
W
in (
3.1
),
by possibly enlarging the probability space
\Omega_{2}
,
there exists a family of translations
\tau_{t_{0}}:\Omega_{2}\to\Omega_{2}
such that

W(t,\tau_{t_{0}}(\omega_{2}))=W(t+t_{0},\omega_{2})-W(t_{0},\omega_{2})

for
t,t_{0}\geq 0
and
\omega_{2}\in\Omega_{2}
.
Denote by
\Phi^{N}(t)
the stochastic flow map
to the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
6.2
)
constructed in Lemma
6.2

(which is not necessarily global at this point).
Namely,

\displaystyle\begin{split}\vec{u}_{N}(t)=(u_{N}(t),\partial_{t}u_{N}(t))&=\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\\
&=\big(\Phi^{N}_{1}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}),\Phi^{N}_{2}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\big)\end{split}

(6.21)

is the solution
to (
6.2
) with

\vec{u}_{N}|_{t=0}=\vec{u}_{0}
, satisfying
\Law(\vec{u}_{0})=\vec{\rho}_{N}
,
and the noise
\xi(\omega_{2})
.
We now
extend
\Phi^{N}(t)
as

\displaystyle\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\big(\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}),\tau_{t}(\omega_{2})\big).

(6.22)

Note that
by the uniqueness of the solution to (
6.2
),
we have

\displaystyle\Phi^{N}(t_{1}+t_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\Phi^{N}(t_{2})\big(\Phi^{N}(t_{1})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}),\tau_{t_{1}}(\omega_{2})\big)=\Phi^{N}(t_{2})\big(\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(t_{1})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\big)

for
t_{1},t_{2}\geq 0

as long as the flow is well defined.

By writing the truncated dynamics (
6.2
)
as a superposition of the deterministic NLW:

\displaystyle\partial_{t}^{2}u_{N}+(1-\Delta)u_{N}-\mathcal{N}_{N}(u_{N})=0,

(6.23)

where
\mathcal{N}_{N}(u_{N})
is as in (
6.19
),
and the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process (for
\partial_{t}u_{N}
):

\displaystyle\partial_{t}(\partial_{t}u_{N})=-\partial_{t}u_{N}+\sqrt{2}\xi,

(6.24)

we see that
the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
in (
6.1
)
is formally
26
26

26

Namely, as long as the dynamics is well defined.

invariant under the dynamics of (
6.2
),
since
\vec{\rho}_{N}
is invariant under the NLW dynamics (
6.23
),
while the white noise measure
\mu_{0}
on
\partial_{t}u_{N}

(and hence
\vec{\rho}_{N}=\rho_{N}\otimes\mu_{0}

on
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})
) is invariant under the
Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics (
6.24
).
Then, by exploiting the formal invariance of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
,
Bourgain’s invariant measure argument
[
9
]

yields the following result on
almost sure global well-posedness of
the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
6.2
)
and invariance of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
.
Since the argument is standard (for fixed
N\in\mathbb{N}
), we omit details.
See the proof of Lemma 9.3 in
[
54
]
for details.

Lemma 6.4
.

Let
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
Then, the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
6.2
) is almost surely globally well-posed
with respect to the random initial data distributed
by the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}
in (
6.1
).
Furthermore,
\vec{\rho}_{N}
is invariant under the resulting dynamics
and, as a consequence, the measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
is invariant
under the extended stochastic flow map
\widehat{\Phi}^{N}(t)
defined in (
6.22
).
More precisely, there exists
\Sigma_{N}\subset\Omega=\Omega_{1}\times\Omega_{2}

with
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\Sigma_{N})=1
such that the solution

u_{N}=u_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
to (
6.2
) exists globally in time
and
\Law(u_{N}(t),\partial_{t}u_{N}(t))=\vec{\rho}_{N}
for any
t\in\mathbb{R}_{+}
.

Next, we establish
uniform exponential integrability of the truncated enhanced data set

\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.10
)
with respect to the truncated measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
.
We also establish
uniform exponential integrability
for the difference of the truncated enhanced data sets.

Proposition 6.5
.

Let
T>0
.
Then,
we have

\displaystyle\int\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{2}}\Big[\exp\Big(\|\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}^{\alpha}\Big)\Big]d\vec{\rho}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0})\leq C(T,\varepsilon,\alpha)<\infty

(6.25)

for
0<\alpha<\frac{1}{3}
,
uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
where the
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
-norm and
the truncated enhanced data set
\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
are as in (
5.49
) and (
6.10
), respectively.
Here,

\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{2}}
denotes an expectation
with respect to
the probability measure
\mathbb{P}_{2}
on
\omega_{2}\in\Omega_{2}

defined in (
6.4
).

Moreover, there exists small
\beta>0
such that

\displaystyle\int\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{2}}\Big[\exp\Big(N_{2}^{\beta}\|\Xi_{N_{1}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})-\Xi_{N_{2}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}^{\alpha}\Big)\Big]d\vec{\rho}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0})\leq C(T,\varepsilon,\alpha)<\infty

(6.26)

for
0<\alpha<\frac{1}{3}
,
uniformly in
N,N_{1},N_{2}\in\mathbb{N}
with
N\geq N_{1}\geq N_{2}
.

Before proceeding further,
we record the following boundedness
of
\mathcal{K}^{\theta}
defined in (
6.29
) and (
6.30
);
a slight modification of the proof of (
2.7
) in Lemma
2.2

yields

\displaystyle\|\mathcal{K}^{\theta}(f,g)\|_{B^{s_{2}}_{p,q}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{p_{1}}}\|g\|_{B^{s_{2}}_{p_{2},q}}

(6.33)

for any
s_{2}\in\mathbb{R}
and
1\leq p,p_{1},p_{2},q\leq\infty
such that

\frac{1}{p}=\frac{1}{p_{1}}+\frac{1}{p_{2}}
.

By the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
)
with the change of variables (
3.12

(6.43)

Note that
(\frac{1}{3\varepsilon},\frac{6}{1-4\varepsilon})
is
(1-\varepsilon)
-admissible.

6.36

5.3

we have

\displaystyle\|\psi_{1}\|_{L_{T}^{q^{\prime}}B^{0}_{\frac{6}{1-4\varepsilon},2}}\leq\bigg(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\|S(t)(\mathbf{P}_{j}\Theta,0)\|_{L_{T}^{q^{\prime}}L^{\frac{6}{1-4\varepsilon}}_{x}}^{2}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{2}}\lesssim\|\Theta\|_{H^{1-\varepsilon}},

(6.44)

The rest of the argument follows
precisely as in Part 1.

) and (

).
