for all the elements in the truncated enhanced data set

\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.10
).

We conclude this subsection by constructing the full enhanced data set

\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.11
) under
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

as a limit of the truncated enhanced data set

\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.10
).

Corollary 6.7
.

Let
T>0
. Then,
the truncated enhanced data set
\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.10
)
converges to
the enhanced data set
\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.11
),
with respect to the
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
-norm defined in (
5.49
),
almost surely and in measure with respect to
the limiting measure
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
.

Proof.

Let
0<\alpha<\frac{1}{3}
and
\beta>0
be as in Proposition
6.5
.
Then, by
Fatou’s lemma, the weak convergence of
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

to
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
,
and Proposition
6.5
, we have

\displaystyle\int

\displaystyle\exp\Big(N_{2}^{\beta}\|\Xi_{N_{1}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})-\Xi_{N_{2}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}^{\alpha}\Big)d(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

\displaystyle\leq\liminf_{L\to\infty}\int\exp\Big(\min\big(N_{2}^{\beta}\|\Xi_{N_{1}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})-\Xi_{N_{2}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}^{\alpha},L\big)\Big)d(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

\displaystyle=\liminf_{L\to\infty}\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\exp\Big(\min\big(N_{2}^{\beta}\|\Xi_{N_{1}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXXXXXXXXX}-\Xi_{N_{2}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}^{\alpha},L\big)\Big)d(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

\displaystyle\leq\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\exp\Big(N_{2}^{\beta}\|\Xi_{N_{1}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})-\Xi_{N_{2}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}^{\alpha}\Big)d(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

\displaystyle\lesssim 1,

(6.56)

uniformly in
N_{1}\geq N_{2}\geq 1
.
Then, by Chebyshev’s inequality, we have

\displaystyle\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\Big(\|\Xi_{N_{1}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})-\Xi_{N_{2}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}^{\alpha}>\lambda\Big)\leq Ce^{-cN_{2}^{\beta}\lambda^{\alpha}}

for any
\lambda>0
and
N_{1}\geq N_{2}\geq 1
.
This shows that
\{\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}

is Cauchy in measure with respect to
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

and thus converges in measure to the full enhanced data set

\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.11
).
By Fatou’s lemma and (
6.56
),
we also have

\displaystyle\int

\displaystyle\exp\Big(N_{2}^{\beta}\|\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})-\Xi_{N_{2}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}^{\alpha}\Big)d(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\lesssim 1,

uniformly in
N_{1}\geq N_{2}\geq 1
, which in turn implies

\displaystyle\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\Big(\|\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})-\Xi_{N_{2}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}^{\alpha}>\lambda\Big)\leq Ce^{-cN_{2}^{\beta}\lambda^{\alpha}}

for any
\lambda>0
and
N_{2}\in\mathbb{N}
.
By summing in
N_{2}\in\mathbb{N}

and invoking the Borel-Cantelli lemma,
we also conclude almost sure convergence

\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
to

\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
with respect to
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
.
∎

6.2.
Proof of Theorem
1.15

In this subsection, we present the proof of Theorem
1.15
.
The main task is to prove convergence of
the solution
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})
to the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
6.2
).
We first carry out Steps 2, 3, and 4
described at the beginning of this section.
Namely,
we first establish
a stability result (Proposition
6.8
)
as a slight modification of
the local well-posedness argument (Theorem
5.1
).
Next, we
establish a uniform (in
N
) control
on the solution
(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})

to the truncated system (see (
6.57
) below)
with respect to the truncated measure
\rho_{N}\times\mathbb{P}_{2}

(Proposition
6.9
).
Then, by using ideas from theory of optimal transport,
we study
the convergence property of
the pushforward measure

(\Xi_{N})_{\#}(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})

to

(\Xi)_{\#}(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})

with respect to the
Wasserstein-1 distance (Proposition
6.10
).

Let
\Phi^{N}_{1}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

be the first component of
\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

in (
6.21
).
Then,
by decomposing
\Phi^{N}_{1}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

as in (
5.11
):

\displaystyle\Phi_{1}^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})+\sigma\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(t;\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})+X_{N}(t)+Y_{N}(t),

(6.57)

we see that

X_{N}
,
Y_{N}
, and
\mathfrak{R}_{N}:=X_{N}\mathbin{{\mathchoice{\scalebox{.7}{{\hbox{\hbox to8.9pt{\vbox to8.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.45pt\lower-4.45pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {}{{}}{}{{}}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{{{}}}{{}}{}{}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{}{}{}{}{}{{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.88 0 C 5.88 3.25 3.25 5.88 0 5.88 C -3.25 5.88 -5.88 3.25 -5.88 0 C -5.88 -3.25 -3.25 -5.88 0 -5.88 C 3.25 -5.88 5.88 -3.25 5.88 0 Z M 0 0}{fill:none} \ignorespaces

Proposition 6.8
.

(6.64)

In the following,

28

The main observation is the following bound:

\displaystyle e^{-\lambda t}\|e^{\lambda t^{\prime}}\|_{L^{q}_{t^{\prime}}([0,t])}\lesssim\lambda^{-\frac{1}{q}}.

(6.65)

Let

be the Duhamel integral operator defined in (

Then, using (

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|e^{-\lambda t}\mathcal{I}(F)\|_{C_{T}H^{s}_{x}}&\leq\bigg\|e^{-\lambda t}\int_{0}^{t}e^{\lambda t^{\prime}}\|e^{-\lambda t^{\prime}}F(t^{\prime})\|_{H^{s-1}_{x}}dt^{\prime}\bigg\|_{L^{\infty}_{T}}\\
&\lesssim\lambda^{-\frac{1}{q}}\|e^{-\lambda t^{\prime}}F(t^{\prime})\|_{L^{q^{\prime}}_{T}H^{s-1}_{x}}\end{split}

),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|e^{-\lambda t}\mathcal{I}(F)\|_{L^{q_{2}}_{T}L^{r_{2}}_{x}}&\leq\bigg\|\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\lambda(t-t^{\prime})}\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})(e^{-\lambda t^{\prime}}F(t^{\prime}))dt^{\prime}\bigg\|_{L^{q_{2}}_{T}L^{r_{2}}_{x}}\\
&\leq\int_{0}^{T}\|\mathcal{D}(t-t^{\prime})(e^{-\lambda t^{\prime}}F(t^{\prime}))\|_{L^{q_{2}}_{t}([0,T];L^{r_{2}}_{x})}dt^{\prime}\\
&\lesssim\|e^{-\lambda t^{\prime}}F(t^{\prime})\|_{L^{1}_{T}H^{s_{2}-1}_{x}}.\end{split}

(6.67)

Thus,
given any
\delta>0
,
it follows from
interpolating (
6.66
)
with large
q\gg 1
and (
6.67
) that
there exists small
\theta=\theta(\delta)>0
such that

\displaystyle\|e^{-\lambda t}\mathcal{I}(F)\|_{L^{q_{1}}_{T}L^{r_{1}}_{x}}

\displaystyle\leq C(T)\lambda^{-\theta}\|e^{-\lambda t^{\prime}}F(t^{\prime})\|_{L^{1+\delta}_{T}H^{s_{1}-1}_{x}}.

(6.68)

Recalling that
(4,4)
is
\frac{1}{2}
-admissible,
it follows from (
6.66
), (
6.68
), and
Sobolev’s inequality that

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|e^{-\lambda t}\mathcal{I}(F)\|_{C_{T}\mathcal{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}_{x}\cap L^{4}_{T}L^{4}_{x}}&\leq C(T)\lambda^{-\theta}\|e^{-\lambda t^{\prime}}F(t^{\prime})\|_{L^{1+\delta}_{T}H^{-\frac{1}{2}}_{x}}\\
&\leq C(T)\lambda^{-\theta}\|e^{-\lambda t^{\prime}}F(t^{\prime})\|_{L^{1+\delta}_{T}L^{\frac{3}{2}}_{x}}.\end{split}

(6.69)

6.58
) in the Duhamel formulation, we have

(i))

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{2}-\frac{1}{2}}(fg)\|_{L^{\frac{3}{2}}}&\lesssim\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{2}-\frac{1}{2}}f\|_{L^{r_{1}}}\|g\|_{L^{r_{2}}}+\|f\|_{L^{r_{2}}}\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{2}-\frac{1}{2}}g\|_{L^{r_{1}}}\\
&\lesssim\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{1}-\frac{1}{4}}f\|_{L^{\frac{8}{3}}}\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{1}-\frac{1}{4}}g\|_{L^{\frac{8}{3}}},\end{split}

(6.81)

provided that
\frac{1}{r_{1}}+\frac{1}{r_{2}}=\frac{2}{3}
with
1<r_{1},r_{2}\leq\infty
,

\displaystyle\frac{s_{1}-s_{2}+\frac{1}{4}}{3}\geq\frac{3}{8}-\frac{1}{r_{1}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{s_{1}-\frac{1}{4}}{3}\geq\frac{3}{8}-\frac{1}{r_{2}}.

(6.82)

This condition is easily satisfied by taking
s_{1}<\frac{1}{2}<s_{2}

both sufficiently close to
\frac{1}{2}
and
r_{1}=r_{2}=3
.
By (
6.69
), (
6.81
), and Lemma
2.3
(i),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\big\|&e^{-\lambda t}\mathcal{I}\big((X_{1}+Y_{1}+\Xi_{0})(X_{2}+Y_{2}+\Xi_{0})\big)\big\|_{Y^{s_{2}}(T)}\\
&\leq C(T)\lambda^{-\theta}\big\|e^{-\lambda t}\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{2}-\frac{1}{2}}\big((X_{1}+Y_{1}+\Xi_{0})(X_{2}+Y_{2}+\Xi_{0})\big)\big\|_{L^{1+\delta}_{T}L^{\frac{3}{2}}_{x}}\\
&\leq C(T)\lambda^{-\theta}\Big(\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{1}-\frac{1}{4}}X_{1}\|_{L^{8}_{T}L^{\frac{8}{3}}_{x}}+\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{2}-\frac{1}{2}}Y_{1}\|_{L^{4}_{T,x}}+\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{2}-\frac{1}{2}}\Xi_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T,x}}\Big)\\
&\quad\times\Big(\|e^{-\lambda t}\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{1}-\frac{1}{4}}X_{2}\|_{L^{8}_{T}L^{\frac{8}{3}}_{x}}+\|e^{-\lambda t}\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{2}-\frac{1}{2}}Y_{2}\|_{L^{4}_{T,x}}+\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{s_{2}-\frac{1}{2}}\Xi_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}_{T,x}}\Big),\end{split}

(6.83)

provided that

s_{1}<\frac{1}{2}<s_{2}

are both sufficiently close to
\frac{1}{2}
.
Compare this with
(
5.54
).
Then, from
(
6.66
), (
6.68
),
and (
6.83
)
with (

),
(
6.60
),
(

), and (

),
a slight modification of (

\displaystyle\|e^{-\lambda t}\text{I \hskip-7.96677pt I}_{3}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}(T)}\leq C(T)\lambda^{-\theta}\Big(R^{4}\|\delta Z_{N}\|_{\mathcal{Z}_{\lambda}^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}+K_{0}^{5}\Big)

(6.84)

for any
\delta Z_{N}\in B_{1}
.

,
or

\displaystyle\leq C(T)(\kappa+N^{-\delta})K_{0}(R^{4}+K_{0}^{4})

\displaystyle\leq K_{0}\Big\|e^{-\lambda t}\|e^{\lambda t^{\prime}}(e^{-\lambda t^{\prime}}(X_{1}+Y_{1}-X_{2}-Y_{2}))\|_{L^{\frac{3}{2}}_{t^{\prime}}([0,t];L^{2}_{x})}\Big\|_{L^{3}_{T}}

.

By a similar computation, we also obtain the difference estimate:

(6.89)

for any

.
We now introduce small

From (

Therefore, by choosing large

for any

.
Hence, there exists a unique solution

to the fixed point problem

.
We need to check that

,

and (

), we have

\displaystyle Z

\displaystyle=\delta Z_{N}+Z_{N}=\vec{\Psi}(\delta Z_{N})+\vec{\Phi}_{N}(Z_{N})

\displaystyle=\vec{\Phi}(\delta Z_{N}+Z_{N})=\vec{\Phi}(Z),

where

.
This shows that

indeed satisfies the Duhamel formulation (

)
with the zero initial data and the enhanced data set

.
Lastly, we point out that

) and

As for the second claim in this proposition,
we write

\displaystyle\delta Z_{N}=\vec{\Psi}^{N}(\delta Z_{N})

\displaystyle\Psi_{j}^{N}

\displaystyle(\delta X_{N},\delta Y_{N},\delta\mathfrak{R}_{N})

\displaystyle=\Phi_{j}(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})-\Phi_{j,N}(X-\delta X_{N},Y-\delta Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}-\delta\mathfrak{R}_{N}).

Next,
we prove that the solution
(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})
to the
truncated system (
6.58
) has a uniform bound with a large probability.
The proof is based on

\vec{\rho}_{N}

under the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
6.2
) (Lemma

)
and a discrete Gronwall argument.

Proposition 6.9
.

Let
T>0
.
Then, given any
\delta>0
, there exists
C_{0}=C_{0}(T,\delta)\gg 1
such that

\displaystyle\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\Big(\|(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}>C_{0}\Big)<\delta,

(6.92)

,
where

is the solution to the truncated system (
6.58
) on

in (

Proof.

Let

be a global solution to (
6.2
) constructed in Lemma

,
where

\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

Then, by the

(Lemma

\displaystyle\int F(\Phi^{N}(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))d(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\int F(\vec{u}_{0})d\rho_{N}(\vec{u}_{0})

.
By Minkowski’s integral inequality, (

),

),

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg\|\int_{0}^{T}&|M(\,:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,)(t)|dt\bigg\|_{L^{p}_{\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}}(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})}\\

&\leq C(T,p)<\infty,\end{split}

(6.94)

for any

and

,
uniformly in

.
By defining

Thus, we have

\displaystyle\|v_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}\leq\int_{0}^{t}\bigg(

\displaystyle\Big\|\frac{\sin((t-t^{\prime})[\hskip-1.70717pt[\nabla]\hskip-1.70717pt])}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[\nabla]\hskip-1.70717pt]}\sigma\pi_{N}(\,:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,)(t^{\prime})\Big\|_{W^{-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}

Then, by using Minkowski’s integral inequality,

we have

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \Big\|\|&v_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}\Big\|_{L^{p}_{\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}}(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})}\\
&\lesssim\int_{0}^{t}\bigg(\Big\|\frac{\sin(\tau[\hskip-1.70717pt[\nabla]\hskip-1.70717pt])}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[\nabla]\hskip-1.70717pt]}\pi_{N}(\,:\!(\pi_{N}u_{0})^{2}\!:\,)\Big\|_{L^{p}_{\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}}(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2};W^{-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x})}\\
&\phantom{XXX}+\Big\|M(\,:\!(\pi_{N}u_{0})^{2}\!:\,)\frac{\sin(\tau[\hskip-1.70717pt[\nabla]\hskip-1.70717pt])}{[\hskip-1.70717pt[\nabla]\hskip-1.70717pt]}\pi_{N}u_{0}\Big\|_{L^{p}_{\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}}(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2};W^{-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x})}\bigg)d\tau\\
&\leq C(T,p)<\infty\end{aligned}

(6.95)

for any

,

, and

uniformly in

We rewrite the system (

&\hphantom{X}+\int_{0}^{T}|M(\,:\!(\pi_{N}u_{N})^{2}\!:\,)(t^{\prime})|\cdot\|\mathbb{A}_{N}(t,t^{\prime})\|_{L^{3}_{t}([t^{\prime},T];H^{s_{3}}_{x})}dt^{\prime}\\
&\leq C(T)K^{2}\Big(K+\|X_{N}\|_{X^{s_{1}}(T)}+\|Y_{N}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}((k+1)\tau)}\Big)+K\int_{0}^{T}L(t)dt.\end{split}

(6.103)

Given
0<t\leq T
,
let
k_{*}(t)
be the largest integer such that
k_{*}(t)\tau\leq t
.
Then, from
(
6.102
) and (
6.103
),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \|&Y_{N}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}(t)}\leq\|Y_{N}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}((k_{*}(t)+1)\tau)}\\
&\leq C(T)K^{2}+C_{1}(T)K^{3}\sum_{k=0}^{k_{*}(t)}\tau^{\frac{2}{3}}\Big(1+\|L(t)\|_{L^{3}_{I_{k}}}\Big)\Big(1+\|X_{N}(t)\|_{X^{s_{1}}(T)}\Big)\\
&\quad+C_{2}KT\sum_{k=0}^{k_{*}(t)}\tau^{\frac{1}{3}}\|L(t)\|_{L^{3}_{I_{k}}}+C_{3}K^{2}\sum_{k=0}^{k_{*}(t)}\tau^{\frac{2}{3}}\Big(1+\|L(t)\|_{L^{3}_{I_{k}}}\Big)\|Y_{N}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}((k+1)\tau)}.\end{aligned}

(6.104)

Now, choose
\tau=\tau(K,L_{1})=\tau(T,\delta)>0
sufficiently small
such that

\displaystyle C_{3}K^{2}\tau^{\frac{2}{3}}L_{1}\ll 1.

(6.105)

In view of (
6.94
) and (
6.95
),
and define
L_{2}=L_{2}(T,\delta)\gg 1
such that

\displaystyle\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\bigg(\sum_{k=0}^{k_{*}(T)}\tau^{\frac{1}{3}}\Big(1+\|L(t)\|_{L^{3}_{I_{k}}}\Big)>L_{2}\bigg)<\frac{\delta}{3}.

(6.106)

In the following,
we work on the set

\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{k_{*}(T)}\tau^{\frac{1}{3}}\Big(1+\|L(t)\|_{L^{3}_{I_{k}}}\Big)\leq L_{2}.

(6.107)

It follows from
(
6.104
) with (
6.100
), (
6.101
),
(
6.105
),
and (
6.107
) that

\displaystyle\|Y_{N}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}((k_{*}(t)+1)\tau)}

\displaystyle\leq C(T)K^{4}L_{1}L_{2}+C_{4}K^{2}\sum_{k=0}^{k_{*}(t)-1}\tau^{\frac{2}{3}}\|L(t)\|_{L^{3}_{I_{k}}}\|Y_{N}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}((k+1)\tau)}.

By applying the discrete Gronwall inequality with (
6.107
), we then obtain

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|Y_{N}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}(t)}&\leq\|Y_{N}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}((k_{*}(t)+1)\tau)}\\
&\leq C(T)K^{4}L_{1}L_{2}\exp\bigg(C_{4}K^{2}\sum_{k=0}^{k_{*}(t)-1}\tau^{\frac{2}{3}}\|L(t)\|_{L^{3}_{I_{k}}}\bigg)\\
&\leq C(T)K^{4}L_{1}L_{2}\exp\big(C_{4}K^{2}L_{2}\big).\end{split}

(6.108)

Therefore, from (
6.101
) and (
6.108
), we have

\displaystyle\|X_{N}\|_{X^{s_{1}}(T)}+\|Y_{N}\|_{Y^{s_{2}}(T)}\leq C(T)KL_{1}+C(T)K^{4}L_{1}L_{2}\exp\big(C_{4}K^{2}L_{2}\big).

Together with (
6.103
), we then obtain

\displaystyle\|(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}\leq C_{5}(T,K,L_{1},L_{2})

under the conditions (
6.100
) and (
6.107
).
Hence, by choosing
C_{0}=C_{0}(T,\delta)>0

in (
6.92
) such that

C_{0}>C_{5}(T,K,L_{1},L_{2})
,
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\bigg(&\big\{\|(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}>C_{0}\big\}\cap\big\{\|\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}\leq K\big\}\\
&\cap\big\{\|L\|_{L^{3}_{T}}\leq L_{1}\big\}\cap\Big\{\sum_{k=0}^{k_{*}(T)}\tau^{\frac{1}{3}}\|L(t)\|_{L^{3}_{I_{k}}}\leq L_{2}\Big\}\bigg)=0.\end{split}

(6.109)

Finally, the bound (
6.92
) follows from
(
6.97
), (
6.99
)
(
6.106
), and (
6.109
).
∎

Given a map
S
from a measure space
(X,\mu)
to a space
Y
,
we use
S_{\#}\mu
to denote the image measure (the pushforward) of
\mu
under
S
.
Fix
T>0
and we set

\displaystyle\nu_{N}=(\Xi_{N})_{\#}(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nu=\Xi_{\#}(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}),

(6.110)

where we view
\Xi_{N}=\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.10
)
and

\Xi=\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.11
)
as maps from

\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega_{2}

to
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
defined in (
5.49
).
In view of the weak convergence of
\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}

to
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
(Theorem
1.8
(i))
and the
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
-almost sure convergence of

\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
to
\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
(Corollary
6.7
),
we see that
\nu_{N}
converges weakly to
\nu
.
Indeed, given a bounded continuous function
F:\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\to\mathbb{R}
,
by the dominated convergence theorem, we have

\displaystyle\bigg|\int

\displaystyle F(\Xi)d\nu_{N}-\int F(\Xi)d\nu\bigg|

\displaystyle=\bigg|\int F(\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))d(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})-\int F(\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))d(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})\bigg|

\displaystyle\leq\|F\|_{L^{\infty}}\bigg|\int 1\,d\big((\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})-(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})\big)\bigg|

\displaystyle\quad+\bigg|\int\big(F(\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))-F(\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))\big)d(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})\bigg|

\displaystyle\longrightarrow 0,

as
N\to\infty
.

Next, we prove that
\nu_{N}=(\Xi_{N})_{\#}(\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})

converges to

\nu=\Xi_{\#}(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})
in the Wasserstein-1 metric.
We view this problem
as
of Kantorovich’s mass optimal transport problem
and study the dual problem under the Kantorovich duality,
using the Boué-Dupuis variational formula.
This proposition plays a crucial role
in the proof of almost sure global well-posedness
and invariance of the Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}

presented at the end of this section.

Proposition 6.10
.

Fix
T>0
.
Then,
there exists a sequence
\{\mathfrak{p}_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}

of probability measures on

\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\times\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}

with the first and second marginals
\nu
and
\nu_{N}
on
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
, respectively,
namely,

\displaystyle\int_{\Xi^{2}\in\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})=d\nu(\Xi^{1})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\int_{\Xi^{1}\in\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})=d\nu_{N}(\Xi^{2}),

(6.111)

such that

\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\times\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}\min(\|\Xi^{1}-\Xi^{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}},1)d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})\longrightarrow 0,

as
N\to\infty
.
Namely, the total transportation cost associated to
\mathfrak{p}_{N}

tends to
0
as
N\to\infty
.

Remark 6.11
.

In view of the weak convergence of the truncated Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}_{N}

to
\vec{\rho}
(Theorem
1.8
)
and the almost sure convergence of the truncated enhanced data set
\Xi_{N}

to
\Xi
with respect to
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}
(Corollary
6.7
),
it suffices to define

\mathfrak{p}_{N}=(\Xi,\Xi_{N})_{\#}(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}).

In the following, however, we present the full proof of Proposition
6.10
,
using the Kantorovich duality and the variational approach
since we believe that such an argument is of general interest.

Proof of Proposition
6.10
.

Define a cost function
c(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})
on
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\times\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}

by setting

\displaystyle c(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})=\min(\|\Xi^{1}-\Xi^{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}},1).

Then, define the Lipschitz norm
for a function
F:\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\to\mathbb{R}
by

\|F\|_{\Lip}=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2}\in\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\\
\Xi^{1}\neq\Xi^{2}\end{subarray}}\frac{|F(\Xi^{1})-F(\Xi^{2})|}{c(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})}.

Note that

\|F\|_{\Lip}\leq 1
implies that

F
is bounded and Lipschitz continuous.
From the Kantorovich duality (the Kantorovich-Rubinstein theorem

[
78
, Theorem 1.14]
),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\inf_{\mathfrak{p}\in\Gamma(\nu,\nu_{N})}\int_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\times\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}c(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})d\mathfrak{p}(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})\\
&\quad=\sup_{\|F\|_{\Lip}\leq 1}\bigg(\int F(\Xi)d\nu_{N}(\Xi)-\int F(\Xi)d\nu(\Xi)\bigg),\end{aligned}

(6.112)

where
\Gamma(\nu,\nu_{N})
is the set of probability measures
on
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\times\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}

with the first and second marginals
\nu
and
\nu_{N}
on
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
, respectively.

For a function
F
with
\|F\|_{\Lip}\leq 1
,
let

G:=F-\inf F+1.

Then, we have

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \int F(\Xi)d\nu_{N}(\Xi)-\int F(\Xi)d\nu(\Xi)&=\int G(\Xi)d\nu_{N}(\Xi)-\int G(\Xi)d\nu(\Xi).\end{aligned}

(6.113)

Note that
\|G\|_{\Lip}=\|F\|_{\Lip}\leq 1
and
1\leq G\leq 2
.
Moreover,
the mean value theorem yields that

\displaystyle\frac{1}{e}\leq\frac{\log x-\log y}{x-y}\leq 1

(6.114)

for any
x,y\in[1,e]
with
x\neq y
.
Set
\{a\}_{+}=\max(a,0)
for any
a\in\mathbb{R}
.
By (
6.113
) and (
6.114
),
we obtain

\displaystyle\begin{split}\int&F(\Xi)d\nu_{N}(\Xi)-\int F(\Xi)d\nu(\Xi)\\
&\lesssim\bigg\{-\log\Big(\int G(\Xi)d\nu(\Xi)\Big)+\log\Big(\int G(\Xi)d\nu_{N}(\Xi)\Big)\bigg\}_{+}\end{split}

(6.115)

for any
N\in\mathbb{N}
.

Finally, define
H=\log G
.
Then, from (
6.114
)
and
1\leq G\leq 2
, we have
\|H\|_{\Lip}\lesssim 1
.
Hence,
it follows from (
6.112
), (
6.113
), and (
6.115
) that

\displaystyle\inf_{\mathfrak{p}\in\Gamma(\nu,\nu_{N})}\int_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\times\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}c(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})d\mathfrak{p}(\Xi^{1},\Xi^{2})

\displaystyle\quad\lesssim\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq H\leq 1\\
\|H\|_{\Lip}\lesssim 1\end{subarray}}\bigg\{-\log\Big(\int\exp(H(\Xi))d\nu(\Xi)\Big)+\log\Big(\int\exp(H(\Xi))d\nu_{N}(\Xi)\Big)\bigg\}_{+}.

Our goal is to show that the right-hand side tends 0 as
N\to\infty.

Since

\|H\|_{\Lip}\lesssim 1
,

H
is bounded and Lipschitz continuous.
Then,
by the weak convergence of
\{\nu_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
to
\nu
,
it suffices to show that

\displaystyle\limsup_{N\to\infty}\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq H\leq 1\\
\|H\|_{\Lip}\lesssim 1\end{subarray}}\sup_{M\geq N}\bigg\{

\displaystyle-\log\Big(\int\exp(H(\Xi))d\nu_{M}(\Xi)\Big)

(6.116)

\displaystyle+\log\Big(\int\exp(H(\Xi))d\nu_{N}(\Xi)\Big)\bigg\}_{+}\leq 0.

From (
6.110
), (
6.1
),
and (
6.114
) with

0\leq H\leq 1
,
we have

\displaystyle\bigg\{

\displaystyle-\log\Big(\int\exp(H(\Xi))d\nu_{M}(\Xi)\Big)+\log\Big(\int\exp(H(\Xi))d\nu_{N}(\Xi)\Big)\bigg\}_{+}

\displaystyle=\bigg\{-\log\Big(\iiint\exp(H(\Xi_{M}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{M}(u_{0})d\mu_{0}(u_{1})d\mathbb{P}_{2}(\omega_{2})\Big)

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXX}+\log\Big(\iiint\exp(H(\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{N}(u_{0})d\mu_{0}(u_{1})d\mathbb{P}_{2}(\omega_{2})\Big)\bigg\}_{+}

\displaystyle\lesssim\bigg\{-\iiint\exp(H(\Xi_{M}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{M}(u_{0})d\mu_{0}(u_{1})d\mathbb{P}_{2}(\omega_{2})

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXX}+\iiint\exp(H(\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{N}(u_{0})d\mu_{0}(u_{1})d\mathbb{P}_{2}(\omega_{2})\bigg\}_{+}

\displaystyle\lesssim\iint\bigg[\Big\{-\int\exp(H(\Xi_{M}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{M}(u_{0})

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXXXX}+\int\exp(H(\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{N}(u_{0})\Big\}_{+}\bigg]d\mu_{0}(u_{1})d\mathbb{P}_{2}(\omega_{2})

\displaystyle\lesssim\iint\bigg[\bigg\{-\log\Big(\int\exp(H(\Xi_{M}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{M}(u_{0})\Big)

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXXXX}+\log\Big(\int\exp(H(\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{N}(u_{0})\Big)\bigg\}_{+}\bigg]d\mu_{0}(u_{1})d\mathbb{P}_{2}(\omega_{2}).

(6.117)

In the following, we study the integrand of the
(u_{1},\omega_{2})
-integral.
Thus, we fix
u_{1}
and
\omega_{2}

and write

\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\Xi_{N}(u_{0},u_{1},\omega_{2})
as
\Xi_{N}(u_{0})

for simplicity of notation.
By the Boué-Dupuis variational formula (Lemma
3.1
)
with the change of variables (
3.12
),
we have

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} -&\log\bigg(\int\exp(H(\Xi_{M}(u_{0})))d\rho_{M}(u_{0})\bigg)+\log\bigg(\int\exp(H(\Xi_{N}(u_{0})))d\rho_{N}(u_{0})\bigg)\\
&=\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{M}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-H(\Xi_{M}(Y+\Upsilon^{M}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M}))+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{M}(Y+\Upsilon^{M}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M})\\
&\hphantom{XXXXXXX}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{M}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]\\
&\phantom{=}-\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-H(\Xi_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N}))+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})\\
&\hphantom{XXXXXXX}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]\\
&\quad+\log Z_{M}-\log Z_{N},\end{aligned}

(6.118)

where
\widehat{R}_{N}^{\diamond}
is as in (
3.33
).
Given

\delta>0
,
let
{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}
be an almost optimizer, namely,

\displaystyle\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-H(\Xi_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N}))+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]

\displaystyle\quad\geq\mathbb{E}\bigg[-H(\Xi_{N}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N}))+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]-\delta.

Then,
by choosing
\Upsilon^{M}={\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}

and the Lipschitz continuity of
H
,
we have

\displaystyle\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{M}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-H(\Xi_{M}(Y+\Upsilon^{M}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M}))+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{M}(Y+\Upsilon^{M}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{M}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]

\displaystyle\hphantom{XX}-\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\mathbb{E}\bigg[-H(\Xi_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N}))+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+\Upsilon^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\bigg]

\displaystyle\hphantom{X}\leq\delta+\mathbb{E}\Big[H(\Xi_{N}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N}))-H(\Xi_{M}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M}))

\displaystyle\phantom{XXXXX}+\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{M}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M})-\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})\Big]

\displaystyle\hphantom{X}\leq\delta+\|H\|_{\Lip}\cdot\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\Xi_{M}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})-\Xi_{N}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M})\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}\Big]

\displaystyle\phantom{XXXXX}+\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{M}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M})-\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})\bigg].

(6.119)

Proceeding as in
Subsection
3.3
with

,
we have (
3.76
).
Then,
using the computations from (

) to (

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{M}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M})-\widehat{R}^{\diamond}_{N}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})\bigg]\longrightarrow 0,

(6.120)

as

.
We also note that as a consequence of (

.

Moreover, by slightly modifying (part of) the proof of Proposition

we can show that

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\mathbb{E}\Big[\big\|\Xi_{M}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{N})-\Xi_{N}(Y+{\underline{\Upsilon}}^{N}+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}_{M})\big\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}\Big]\longrightarrow 0,\end{aligned}

.

Note that
\{Z_{N}\}_{N\in\mathbb{N}}
is a convergent sequence and
\delta>0

Hence, it follows from (
6.118
), (
6.119
), (
6.120
), and (
6.122
) that

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \limsup_{N\to\infty}\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq H\leq 1\\
\|H\|_{\Lip}\lesssim 1\end{subarray}}\sup_{M\geq N}&\bigg\{-\log\bigg(\int\exp(H(\Xi_{M}(u_{0},u_{1},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{M}(u_{0})\bigg)\\
&\qquad+\log\bigg(\int\exp(H(\Xi_{N}(u_{0},u_{1},\omega_{2})))d\rho_{N}(u_{0})\bigg)\bigg\}_{+}\leq 0,\end{aligned}

(6.128)

for almost every
u_{1}
and
\omega_{2}
,
where the supremum in
H
was trivially dropped in the last step of (
6.119
).
Therefore, (
6.116
) follows from
(
6.117
) and (
6.128
)
with
Fatou’s lemma.
This concludes the proof of Proposition
6.10
.
∎

Finally, we present the proof of Theorem
1.15
.

Proof of Theorem
1.15
.

\bullet

Part 1:

We first prove almost sure global well-posedness
of the hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model.
As in
[
9
,
19
,
5
]
,
it suffices to prove “almost” almost sure global well-posedness.
More precisely,
it suffices to prove that given any
T>0
and small
\delta>0
,
there exists
\Sigma_{T,\delta}\subset\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega_{2}

with
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\Sigma_{T,\delta}^{c})<\delta

such that for each

(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{T,\delta}
,
the solution

(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})
to (
5.28
), with
the zero initial data and
the enhanced data
\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega)
in (
6.11
),
exists on the time interval
[0,T]
.

We assume this
“almost” almost sure global well-posedness
claim for the moment.
Denote by

(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})

the solution to the truncated system (
6.58
) with
the truncated enhanced data
\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega)
in (
6.10
)
and set

\displaystyle u_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})+\sigma\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})+X_{N}+Y_{N},

(6.129)

which is the solution to the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
6.2
)
with the initial data
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})|_{t=0}=\vec{u}_{0}=(u_{0},u_{1})

and the noise
\xi=\xi(\omega_{2})
.
Here, we used the uniqueness of the solution
u_{N}

to (
6.2
); see Remark
6.3
.
Then, we
conclude from Corollary
6.7
(on the almost sure convergence
of
\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega)
to
\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega)
)
and the second part of Proposition
6.8

that
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.129
) converges to
(u,\partial_{t}u)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

in
C([0,T];\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))

for each

(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{T,\delta}
,
where
u(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
is defined by

\displaystyle u(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\makebox[5.9748pt][c]{\hbox to5.9748pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.8284pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})+\sigma\makebox[7.79742pt][c]{\hbox to7.79742pt{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=9.64677pt,depth=0.0pt\hskip-3.0pt\hbox{\pdfrefxform}\hss}}(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})+X+Y.

(6.130)

Now, we define

\Sigma=\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty}\bigcap_{j=1}^{\infty}\Sigma_{2^{j},2^{-j}k^{-1}}.

Then, we have
\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\Sigma)=1

and, for each
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma
,
the solution
(u_{N},\partial_{t}u_{N})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

to the truncated hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model (
6.2
)
converges to
(u,\partial_{t}u)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
in (
6.130
)
in

(endowed with the compact-open topology in time).
This proves the almost sure global well-posedness claim in Theorem
1.15
,
assuming
“almost” almost sure global well-posedness.

We now prove
“almost” almost sure global well-posedness.
Fix
T>0
and small
\delta>0
.
Given
\Xi=(\Xi_{1},\dots,\Xi_{6})\in\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
,
let
Z(\Xi)=(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})(\Xi)
be the solution to (

)

\Xi
,
namely,
\Xi_{j}
replacing the
j
th element in (

).
Note that
\Xi
here
denotes a general element in
\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
and
is not associated with
any specific
(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega_{2}
.
Similarly, given
N\in\mathbb{N}
and
\Xi\in\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}
,
let

Z_{N}(\Xi)=(X_{N},Y_{N},\mathfrak{R}_{N})(\Xi)
be the solution to (

)
with the enhanced data set

,
namely,
\Xi_{j}
replacing the

in (

).

Given

,

(6.131)

Let

.
Given

,
we set

\displaystyle A_{N,K,C_{0}}

\displaystyle=\big\{\Xi^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}:\|\Xi^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}\leq K,\,\|Z_{N}(\Xi^{\prime})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}\leq C_{0}\big\}

(6.132)

and

\displaystyle B_{N,K,C_{0}}=\big\{(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})\in\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\times\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}:\|\Xi-\Xi^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}\leq\kappa,\ \Xi^{\prime}\in A_{N,K,C_{0}}\big\},

where

Then, from the stability result (the first claim in Proposition

)
with (
6.131
), (
6.132
), and (
6.133
),
there exists
small
\kappa(T,K,C_{0})\in(0,1)
and

such that

\displaystyle\Sigma_{C_{0}}\times\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}\supset B_{N,K,C_{0}}

(6.134)

for any

.

Let
C_{0}=C_{0}(T,\delta)\gg 1
be as in Proposition
6.9

and let
\mathfrak{p}_{N}
,

, be as in Proposition
6.10
.
Then,
from
(
6.110
),
(
6.111
),
and (

), we have

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \vec{\rho}&\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\big(\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{C_{0}}\big)=\int\mathbf{1}_{\Xi\in\Sigma_{C_{0}}}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})\\
&\geq\int\mathbf{1}_{B_{N,K,C_{0}}}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})\\
&\geq 1-\int\mathbf{1}_{\{\|\Xi-\Xi^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}>\kappa\}}d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})-\int\mathbf{1}_{A_{N,K,C_{0}}^{c}}(\Xi^{\prime})d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})\\
&\geq 1-\frac{1}{\kappa}\int\min(\|\Xi-\Xi^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}},1)d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})-\vec{\rho}_{N}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}(\{\Xi_{N}(\vec{u}_{0}^{\prime},\omega_{2}^{\prime})\in A_{N,K,C_{0}}^{c}\})\\
&>1-\frac{1}{\kappa}\int\min(\|\Xi-\Xi^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}},1)d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})-2\delta,\end{aligned}

(6.135)

where the last step follows from Proposition

by choosing

, together with Proposition

.
By Proposition

,
we have

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\kappa}\int\min(\|\Xi-\Xi_{N}^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}},1)d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi_{N}^{\prime})\longrightarrow 0,

as

.
Therefore, we conclude from

) and (

) that

\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2}\big(\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{C_{0}}\big)>1-2\delta.

This proves “almost” almost sure global well-posedness
with

\Sigma_{T,\delta}=\{(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\mathcal{H}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{T}^{3})\times\Omega_{2}:\Xi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})\in\Sigma_{C_{0}}\},

and hence almost sure global well-posedness
of the hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-model,
namely, the unique limit

in (

.

\bullet

Part 2:

Next, we prove invariance of the Gibbs measure
\vec{\rho}=\rho\otimes\mu_{0}

under the limiting hyperbolic
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-dynamics.
In the following, we prove

\displaystyle\int F(\Phi(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))d(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})=\int F(\vec{u}_{0})d\vec{\rho}(\vec{u}_{0})

for any bounded Lipschitz functional

and

,
where
\Phi(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})
is the limit
of the solution

to the truncated hyperbolic

-model
defined in (

).

As in Part 1, we use the notation

(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})=(X,Y,\mathfrak{R})(\Xi)
, etc.
Also,
let
\mathfrak{p}_{N}
,

, be as in Proposition

.
Then, by

) (also for

),

), (

),
and the invariance of

we have

\displaystyle\int

\displaystyle F(\Phi(t)(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2}))d(\vec{\rho}\otimes\mathbb{P}_{2})(\vec{u}_{0},\omega_{2})

\displaystyle=\int F(\Phi(t)(\Xi))d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\int F(\Phi^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime}))d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})+\int\big[F(\Phi(t)(\Xi))-F(\Phi^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime}))\big]d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})

\displaystyle=\int F(\vec{u}_{0})d\vec{\rho}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0})+\int\big[F(\Phi(t)(\Xi))-F(\Phi^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime}))\big]d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime}).

By the weak convergence of
\vec{\rho}_{N}
to
\vec{\rho}
, we have

\lim_{N\to\infty}\int F(\vec{u}_{0})d\vec{\rho}_{N}(\vec{u}_{0})=\int F(\vec{u}_{0})d\vec{\rho}(\vec{u}_{0}).

Hence, since

F
is bounded and Lipschitz,
(
6.137
) is reduced to showing that

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\int\min\big(\|\Phi(t)(\Xi)-\Phi^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime})\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-100}\times\mathcal{C}^{-100}},1\big)d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})\longrightarrow 0,\end{aligned}

(6.138)

as
N\to\infty
.

As in (
6.21
),
we write

\Phi(t)(\Xi)=\big(\Phi_{1}(t)(\Xi),\Phi_{2}(t)(\Xi)\big)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Phi^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime})=\big(\Phi_{1}^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime}),\Phi_{2}^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime})\big),

where
\Xi=(\Xi_{1},\dots,\Xi_{6})
and

) and (

With the decomposition as in

), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\Phi_{1}(t)(\Xi)&=\Xi_{1}+\sigma\Xi_{3}+X(\Xi)+Y(\Xi),\\
\Phi_{1}^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime})&=\Xi_{1}^{\prime}+\sigma\Xi_{3}^{\prime}+X_{N}(\Xi^{\prime})+Y_{N}(\Xi^{\prime}),\end{split}

(6.139)

and
\Phi_{2}(t)(\Xi)=\partial_{t}\Phi_{1}(t)(\Xi)
and
\Phi_{2}^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime})=\partial_{t}\Phi_{1}^{N}(t)(\Xi^{\prime})

are given by term-by-term differentiation
of the terms on the right-hand sides of (

).
From the definition (

) of the

-norm,
we clearly have

\displaystyle\|(

\displaystyle\Xi_{1}+\sigma\Xi_{3})(t)-(\Xi_{1}^{\prime}+\sigma\Xi_{3}^{\prime})(t)\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-100}}

\displaystyle+\|(\partial_{t}\Xi_{1}+\sigma\partial_{t}\Xi_{3})(t)-(\partial_{t}\Xi_{1}^{\prime}+\sigma\partial_{t}\Xi_{3}^{\prime})(t)\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-100}}\lesssim\|\Xi-\Xi^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}.

Hence, in view of (
5.32
) with (
5.47
),
(
6.138
) is reduced to showing that

\displaystyle\int\min\big(\|Z(\Xi)-Z_{N}(\Xi^{\prime})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)},1\big)d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})\longrightarrow 0,

as

,
where

and

as in Part 1.

It follows from the second part of

(with

and

that

\displaystyle\int

\displaystyle\min\big(\|Z(\Xi)-Z_{N}(\Xi^{\prime})\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)},1\big)d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})

\displaystyle\leq A\big(T,\|\Xi\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}},\|Z(\Xi)\|_{Z^{s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}}(T)}\big)

\displaystyle\quad\times\int\min\big(\|\Xi-\Xi^{\prime}\|_{\mathcal{X}^{\varepsilon}_{T}}+N^{-\delta},1\big)d\mathfrak{p}_{N}(\Xi,\Xi^{\prime})\longrightarrow 0,

.
This proves (

and therefore,

which proves invariance of the Gibbs measure

under the limiting hyperbolic

Appendix A
Absolute continuity with respect to the shifted measure

A.1.
Preliminary lemmas

In this appendix,
we prove that the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
\rho
in the weakly nonlinear regime
(
|\sigma|\ll 1
),
constructed in Theorem
1.8
(i),
is absolutely continuous
with respect to the shifted measure
\Law(Y(1)+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}(1)+\mathcal{W}(1))
,
where
Y
is as in (
3.2
),
\mathfrak{Z}
is defined as the limit of
the antiderivative of

\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}^{N}
in (
3.11
) as
N\to\infty
, and the auxiliary process
\mathcal{W}
is defined by

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}(t)=(1-\Delta)^{-1}\int_{0}^{t}\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}\big(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}Y(t^{\prime})\big)^{5}dt^{\prime}

(A.1)

for some small
\varepsilon>0
.
For the proof,
we construct a drift as in the discussion in Section 3 of
[
4
]
.
See also Appendix C in
[
54
]
.
The coercive term
\mathcal{W}
is introduced to
guarantee global existence of a drift on the time interval
[0,1]
.
See Lemma
A.2
below.
We closely follow the presentation in Appendix C of our previous work
[
54
]
.

First, we recall the following general lemma,
giving a criterion for absolute continuity.
See Lemma C.1 in
[
54
]
for the proof.

Lemma A.1
.

Let
\mu_{n}
and
\rho_{n}
be probability measures on a Polish space
X
.
Suppose that
\mu_{n}
and
\rho_{n}
converge weakly to
\mu
and
\rho
, respectively.
Furthermore, suppose that for every
\varepsilon>0
,
there exist
\delta(\varepsilon)>0
and
\eta(\varepsilon)>0

with
\delta(\varepsilon)
,
\eta(\varepsilon)\to 0
as
\varepsilon\to 0
such that for every continuous function
F:X\to\mathbb{R}
with
0<\inf F\leq F\leq 1
satisfying

\mu_{n}(\{F\leq\varepsilon\})\geq 1-\delta(\varepsilon)

for any
n\geq n_{0}(F)
,
we have

\displaystyle\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int F(u)d\rho_{n}(u)\leq\eta(\varepsilon).

Then,
\rho
is absolutely continuous with respect to
\mu
.

By regarding

\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}^{N}
in (
3.11
) and
\mathcal{W}
in (
A.1
)
as functions of
Y
,
we write them as

\displaystyle\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}^{N}(Y)(t)

\displaystyle=(1-\Delta)^{-1}\!:\!Y_{N}^{2}(t)\!:\,,

(A.2)

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}(Y)(t)

\displaystyle=(1-\Delta)^{-1}\int_{0}^{t}\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}\big(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}Y(t^{\prime})\big)^{5}dt^{\prime}

and we set
\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}(Y)=\pi_{N}\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}^{N}(Y)
.
Then, from
(
A.2
), we have

\displaystyle\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}(Y+\Theta)-\dot{\mathfrak{Z}}_{N}(Y)=(1-\Delta)^{-1}\pi_{N}(2\Theta_{N}Y_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2}),

(A.3)

where
\Theta_{N}=\pi_{N}\Theta
.
We also define
\mathcal{W}_{N}(Y)(t)
by

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{N}(Y)(t)

\displaystyle=(1-\Delta)^{-1}\pi_{N}\int_{0}^{t}\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}\big(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}Y_{N}(t^{\prime})\big)^{5}dt^{\prime}.

(A.4)

Next, we state a lemma on the construction of a drift
\Theta
.

Lemma A.2
.

Let
\sigma\in\mathbb{R}
and
\dot{\Upsilon}\in L^{2}([0,1];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
.
Then, given any
N\in\mathbb{N}
,
the Cauchy problem for
\Theta
:

\begin{cases}\dot{\Theta}+\sigma(1-\Delta)^{-1}\pi_{N}(2\Theta_{N}Y_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2})+\dot{\mathcal{W}}_{N}(Y+\Theta)-\dot{\Upsilon}=0\\
\Theta(0)=0\end{cases}

(A.5)

is almost surely globally well-posed
on the time interval
[0,1]

such that a solution
\Theta
belongs to
C([0,1];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
.
Moreover, if
\|\dot{\Upsilon}\|^{2}_{L^{2}([0,\tau];H^{1}_{x})}\leq M
for some
M>0

and for some stopping time
\tau\in[0,1]
,
then, for any
1\leq p<\infty
, there exists

such that

\mathbb{E}\Big[\|\dot{\Theta}\|_{L^{2}([0,\tau];H^{1}_{x})}^{p}\Big]\leq C(M,p),

(A.6)

where
C(M,p)
is independent of
N\in\mathbb{N}
.

A.2.
Absolute continuity

In this subsection, we
prove the absolute continuity of

\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure

For simplicity, we use the same short-hand notations as in

In view of Lemma

\displaystyle\hphantom{XXXXX}+\frac{M}{20}\mathbb{P}\bigg(\{\tau_{M}<1\}\cap\bigg\{\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Theta}^{N}_{M}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt<2C(M,2)\bigg\}\bigg)\Bigg\}-C_{1}.

In view of (

),
Markov’s inequality gives

\mathbb{P}\bigg(\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Theta}^{N}_{M}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt=\int_{0}^{\tau_{M}}\|\dot{\Theta}^{N}_{M}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt\geq 2C(M,2)\bigg)\leq\frac{1}{2},

which yields

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(\{\tau_{M}<1\}\cap\bigg\{\int_{0}^{1}\|\dot{\Theta}^{N}_{M}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{2}dt<2C(M,2)\bigg\}\bigg)\geq\mathbb{P}(\{\tau_{M}<1\})-\frac{1}{2}.

(A.18)

Now, we set
M=20L
.
Note from
(
A.10
) that
\mathbb{P}(\{\tau_{M}=1\})+\mathbb{P}(\{\tau_{M}<1\})=1
.
Then,
from (
A.17
) and (
A.18
),
we obtain

\displaystyle-\log

\displaystyle\bigg(\int\exp(-G(u)-R^{\diamond}_{N}(u))d\mu(u)\bigg)

\displaystyle\geq\inf_{\dot{\Upsilon}^{N}\in\mathbb{H}_{a}^{1}}\bigg\{L\Big(\mathbb{P}(\{\tau_{M}=1\})-C^{\prime}_{L}\delta(L)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big)+L\Big(\mathbb{P}(\{\tau_{M}<1\})-\frac{1}{2}\Big)\bigg\}-C_{1}

\displaystyle=L\Big(\frac{1}{2}-C_{L}^{\prime}\delta(L)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big)-C_{1}.

Therefore,
by choosing
\delta(L)>0
such that
C^{\prime}_{L}\delta(L)^{\frac{1}{2}}\to 0
as
L\to\infty
,
this shows (
A.8
) with

R(L)=L\Big(\frac{1}{2}-C^{\prime}_{L}\delta(L)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big)-C_{1}+\log Z,

where
Z=\lim_{N\to\infty}Z_{N}
denotes the
limit of the partition functions for the truncated
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measures
\rho_{N}
.

A.3.
Proof of Lemma
A.2

We conclude this appendix by presenting the proof of Lemma
A.2
.

Proof of Lemma
A.2
.

By Lemma
2.3
(ii) and Sobolev’s inequality,
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|(1-\Delta)^{-1}(2\Theta_{N}Y_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2})(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}&\lesssim\|(2\Theta_{N}Y_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2})(t)\|_{H^{-1}_{x}}\\
&\lesssim\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{H^{\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon}_{x}}\|Y_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}+\|\Theta_{N}^{2}(t)\|_{L_{x}^{\frac{6}{5}}}\\
&\lesssim\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}\|Y_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}+\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{H_{x}^{1}}^{2}\end{split}

(A.19)

for small
\varepsilon>0
.
Moreover,
from (
A.1
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\dot{\mathcal{W}}_{N}(Y(t)+\Theta(t))\|_{H^{1}_{x}}&\lesssim\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}Y_{N}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}_{x}}^{5}+\|\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}_{x}}^{5}\\
&\lesssim\|Y_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}^{5}+\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}_{x}}^{5}.\end{split}

(A.20)

Therefore,
by studying the integral formulation of
(
A.5
),
a contraction argument
in
L^{\infty}([0,T];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{3}))
for small
T>0

with (
A.19
) and (
A.20
)
yields local well-posedness.
Here, the local existence time
T
depends on

\|\Theta(0)\|_{H^{1}}
,

\|\dot{\Upsilon}\|_{L^{2}_{T}H^{1}_{x}}
, and

\|Y_{N}\|_{L^{6}_{T}W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,\infty}_{x}}
,
where the last term is almost surely bounded in view of Lemma
3.2

and (
2.4
).

Next, we prove global existence on
[0,1]

by establishing an a priori bound on the
H^{1}
-norm of a solution.
From (
A.5
) with (
A.4
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|\Theta(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}&=-\sigma\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(2\Theta_{N}(t)Y_{N}(t)+\Theta_{N}^{2}(t))\Theta_{N}(t)dx\\
&\quad-\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\big(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(Y_{N}(t)+\Theta_{N}(t))\big)^{5}\cdot\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}\Theta_{N}(t)dx\\
&\quad+\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\langle\nabla\rangle\Theta(t)\cdot\langle\nabla\rangle\dot{\Upsilon}(t)dx.\end{split}

(A.21)

The second term on the right-hand side of (
A.21
),
coming from
\mathcal{W}
is a coercive term,
allowing us to hide part of the first term on the right-hand side.

From Lemma
2.1

and Young’s inequality,
we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\bigg|\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}&(2\Theta_{N}(t)Y_{N}(t)+\Theta_{N}^{2}(t))\Theta_{N}(t)dx\bigg|\\
&\lesssim\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{L^{3}}^{3}+\|Y_{N}(t)\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{c}\end{split}

(A.22)

for small
\varepsilon>0
and some
c>0
.
We now estimate the second term on the right-hand side of (
A.22
).
By (
2.3
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{L^{3}}^{3}&\lesssim\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{\frac{3+6\varepsilon}{3+2\varepsilon}}\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,6}}^{\frac{6}{3+2\varepsilon}}\\
&\leq\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\varepsilon_{0}\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,6}}^{6}+C_{\varepsilon_{0}}\end{split}

(A.23)

for small
\varepsilon,\varepsilon_{0}>0
.
As for the coercive term, from (
3.40
) and Young’s inequality, we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}&\big(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}(Y_{N}(t)+\Theta_{N}(t))\big)^{5}\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}\Theta_{N}(t)dx\\
&\geq\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}\Theta_{N}(t))^{6}dx-c\int_{\mathbb{T}^{3}}\big|(\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}Y_{N}(t))^{5}\langle\nabla\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}\Theta_{N}(t)\big|dx\\
&\geq\frac{1}{2}\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,6}}^{6}-c\|Y_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,6}}^{5}\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,6}}\\
&\geq\frac{1}{4}\|\Theta_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,6}}^{6}-c\|Y_{N}(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,6}}^{6}.\end{split}

(A.24)

Therefore, putting (
A.21
), (
A.22
), (
A.23
), and (
A.24
) together
we obtain

\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\|\Theta(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}

\displaystyle\lesssim\|\Theta(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|\dot{\Upsilon}(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}+\|Y(t)\|_{\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}}^{c}+\|Y(t)\|_{W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,6}}^{6}+1.

By Gronwall’s inequality, we then obtain

\displaystyle\|\Theta(t)\|_{H^{1}}^{2}\lesssim\|\dot{\Upsilon}\|_{L^{2}([0,t];H^{1}_{x})}^{2}+\|Y_{N}\|_{L^{c}([0,1];\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}_{x})}^{c}+\|Y\|_{L^{6}([0,1];W^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon,6}_{x})}^{6}+1,

(A.25)

uniformly in
0\leq t\leq 1
.
The a priori bound (
A.25
) together with Lemma
3.2
allows us to iterate
the local well-posedness argument,
guaranteeing existence of the solution
\Theta
on
[0,1]
.

Lastly, we prove the bound (
A.6
).
From (
A.19
), (
A.20
),
and (
A.25
), we have

\displaystyle\begin{split}\|\sigma(1&-\Delta)^{-1}(2\Theta_{N}Y_{N}+\Theta_{N}^{2})+\dot{\mathcal{W}}_{N}(Y+\Theta)\|_{L^{2}([0,\tau];H^{1}_{x})}\\
&\lesssim\|\dot{\Upsilon}\|_{L^{2}([0,\tau];H^{1}_{x})}^{5}+\|Y_{N}\|_{L^{q}([0,1];\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon}_{x})}^{c_{0}}+1\end{split}

(A.26)

for some finite
q,c_{0}\geq 1

and for any
0\leq\tau\leq 1
.
Then, using the equation (
A.5
), the bound (
A.6
)
follows from (
A.26
), the bound on
\dot{\Upsilon}
,
and the following corollary to
Lemma
3.2
:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\|Y_{N}\|_{L^{q}([0,1];\mathcal{C}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon}_{x})}^{p}\Big]<\infty

for any finite
p,q\geq 1
, uniformly in
N\in\mathbb{N}
.
∎

Remark A.3
.

A slight modification of the argument presented above shows that
the tamed
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure
\nu_{\delta}
constructed in Proposition

4.1

is
absolutely continuous
with respect to the shifted measure
\Law(Y(1)+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}(1)+\mathcal{W}(1))
.
In this setting, we can use the analysis
in Subsection
4.2

(Step 1 of the proof of Proposition
4.1
)
to arrive at
(
A.9
). The rest of the argument remains unchanged.
As a consequence, the
\sigma
-finite version
\overline{\rho}_{\delta}
of
the
\Phi^{3}_{3}
-measure defined in (
4.9
)
is also
absolutely continuous
with respect to the shifted measure
\Law(Y(1)+\sigma\mathfrak{Z}(1)+\mathcal{W}(1))

for any
\delta>0
.
